items.title: Economic Fighters League criticises approval of 6 mining leases, calls for bigger state stake in Ghana’s gold
items.description: The Economic Fighters League (EFL) has criticised Parliament’s ratification of six mining leases, accusing the government of handing over Ghana’s mineral wealth to private companies while failing to secure greater benefits for the country. In a statement issued on August 5, after Parliament approved the leases, the pressure group claimed the agreements would allow mining companies to extract gold from more than 300 square kilometres of land for up to 25 years without delivering sufficient returns to the Ghanaian people. “Parliament has just signed away Ghana’s gold for another quarter of a century. Six mining leases. Over 300 square kilometres of Ghanaian land. Up to 25 years of extraction.” The group questioned the government’s assurances that the mining agreements would generate significant economic benefits, arguing that previous deals had failed to improve the lives of communities affected by mining. “We have heard this story before,” the statement said. “Communities are left with polluted rivers, degraded forests, abandoned pits, broken promises and poverty, while billions of dollars in gold leave our shores.” A key concern raised by the EFL was the government’s decision not to renegotiate the State’s equity in the Damang Mine. The group argued that increasing the State’s stake from 10 per cent to at least 50 per cent would have ensured that more of the country’s mineral wealth remained in Ghana. “Most shocking of all is Government’s refusal to renegotiate the State’s equity in the Damang Mine from 10% to at least 50%,” the statement said. “That single decision represents a colossal transfer of wealth from the Ghanaian people to private interests.” According to the EFL, Ghana continues to negotiate mining agreements from a position of weakness despite being one of Africa’s leading gold producers. “A nation rich in gold continues to negotiate like a poor tenant on its own land,” the group stated. The EFL also rejected arguments that greater national ownership of large-scale mining operations is unrealistic because of the high cost of mining equipment and limited technical expertise. “Whenever we demand national ownership or, at the very least, a controlling stake, we are told the machinery is too expensive, and the expertise is beyond us,” it said. The group questioned why Ghana could not invest in building its own mining capacity. “Exactly how expensive are these machines that a sovereign nation of over 35 million people cannot buy anywhere in the world?” the statement asked. It proposed a four-year moratorium on new large-scale mining concessions to allow the country to develop local expertise through specialised mining and mineral engineering programmes. “If the obstacle is technical know-how, why not declare a four-year moratorium on new large-scale concessions, establish specialised mining and mineral engineering programmes, and train the brilliant young Ghanaians who every year demonstrate extraordinary talent in our schools and national science and quiz competitions?” the group said. “Nations are not built by importing competence forever. They are built by creating it.” The EFL also expressed concern that some of the newly approved leases affect forest reserves. It criticised Parliament for approving the agreements despite acknowledging the environmental concerns. “Even Parliament’s own committee admits that some of these leases affect forest reserves, yet proceeds to ratify them while merely asking regulators to ‘strictly enforce’ safeguards,” the statement said. “Ghanaians have seen how that movie ends.” The group reiterated its opposition to what it described as Ghana’s extractive model of development, arguing that the country’s mineral resources should be used to drive industrialisation rather than exporting raw materials. “The Economic Fighters League rejects this extractive model of development,” it said. “Our minerals must finance industrialisation, not perpetual dependency.” The EFL called for future mining agreements to guarantee majority national ownership, local value addition, transparent contracts, legally binding community benefit agreements and stronger environmental safeguards. “Ghana does not need more mining leases. Ghana needs ownership, beneficiation and economic sovereignty. Our gold belongs to the people, not to corporations with 25-year licences to export our future.”

items.title: Osun Election: Obi raises concern over EFCC account freeze, warns against political intimidation
items.description: The presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress Peter Obi, has expressed concern over the reported freezing of the Osun State Government’s bank accounts by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), warning against the use of state institutions to influence electoral processes. Obi, in a statement posted on his official X handle, said he supports a strong fight against corruption but cautioned that such efforts must not become instruments for political intimidation or suppression of democracy. The EFCC had reportedly obtained a court order freezing Osun State Government accounts days before the state’s governorship election. Reacting to the development, Obi said the timing of the action raised questions that needed to be addressed in the interest of public confidence and democratic integrity. “I have always supported a relentless fight against corruption. However, that fight must never become a tool for political intimidation or the suppression of democracy,” he said. The former presidential candidate stressed that no institution, regardless of its importance, should operate in a manner that creates the impression of interfering with the electoral process. According to him, if investigations into alleged wrongdoing had been ongoing for months, taking such a major step close to an election date required explanation. “The timing of this action raises legitimate questions. If investigations had been ongoing for months, why take such a drastic step on the eve of an election? In a democracy, institutions must not only be impartial but must also be seen to be impartial,” Obi stated. He expressed concern over what he described as a growing perception that state institutions were being used to achieve political objectives and secure power. Obi warned that while governments may change, the loss of credibility and independence by public institutions would have serious consequences for the country. “If there is evidence of wrongdoing, the Constitution provides a clear path: seek the appropriate orders from a competent court. Due process is the foundation of justice. No agency should exercise powers beyond those granted by law,” he said. He urged relevant authorities to act strictly within the provisions of the Constitution and ensure that nothing undermines the credibility of the Osun governorship election. Obi called on stakeholders to allow the people of Osun State to freely determine their future through the ballot without intimidation or institutional interference. “Nigeria’s democracy was built on sacrifice. We must not allow it to be weakened by the misuse of institutions or the pursuit of political advantage,” he added. Ghana has not honoured ‘Departed 8’ enough in galamsey fight – Ashigbey
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Chamber of Mines, Dr Kenneth Ashigbey, has expressed disappointment over what he describes as the slow pace of Ghana’s fight against illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, a year after the military helicopter crash that claimed the lives of eight people. The Ghana Armed Forces helicopter crashed on August 6, 2025, while transporting government officials and military personnel on an official assignment, prompting renewed calls for a tougher crackdown on illegal mining across the country. Following the tragedy, government announced a series of measures aimed at intensifying the fight against galamsey, including efforts to dismantle illegal mining networks, prosecute financiers and kingpins, and protect the country’s forests and water bodies. Despite those commitments, concerns have persisted over the pace of enforcement, with environmental advocates continuing to raise alarm over the condition of major rivers and the limited number of successful prosecutions involving alleged illegal mining kingpins. Speaking on Citi FM on Thursday, August 6, to mark the first anniversary of the crash, Dr Ashigbey said Ghana had not done enough to honour the memory of the victims through decisive action against illegal mining. “If you look at our fight against galamsey, we can’t say that we have honoured these eight people as well as we ought to. I remember I said in an interview that the incident was going to result in a situation where there was going to be a drastic change in the galamsey fight, and the Minister for Foreign Affairs said that they had had a Cabinet meeting and that the president was going to come up with a renewed way of fighting it. “But unfortunately, it is interesting that there is only one galamsey kingpin that has been successfully prosecuted and convicted, and we don’t see others being prosecuted, yet the turbidity of our waters is still where they are, and so I think that we have not honoured these eight people enough.”

items.title: 2027: Kwankwaso Group unveils strategy to curb vote buying, boost S’East turnout
items.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — The Kwankwaso National Network (KNN) has said it has developed what it described as “water-tight” measures to tackle vote buying, protect the integrity of the ballot and increase voter participation across the five South-East states ahead of the 2027 general elections. The group also disclosed that it has mobilised its members and grassroots structures across the region to monitor the activities of politicians before, during and after the elections, insisting that every legitimate vote cast by the electorate must count. The South-East Coordinator of KNN, Dr Ukpai Iro Ukpai, disclosed this in a statement made available to journalists in Umuahia. According to him, the group has commenced extensive voter education campaigns aimed at sensitising eligible voters on the dangers of selling their votes, describing vote buying as one of the biggest threats to credible elections and good governance. “We have educated our members and supporters across the South-East on how to resist inducement and reject every attempt by desperate politicians to compromise their conscience through vote buying,” the statement said. The group warned voters against exchanging their future for temporary financial benefits, urging them to consider the long-term implications of their choices at the polls. “It is time for our people to reject momentary gains and refuse to mortgage the future of their children and generations yet unborn for a few pieces of silver. “The choices made in 2027 will shape the destiny of Nigeria for many years, and every voter must approach the election with that sense of responsibility,” it said. KNN further stated that it had concluded plans to collaborate with relevant stakeholders and partners to encourage what it described as unprecedented voter participation across the South-East. The group said it was targeting over 80 per cent voter turnout from the more than 10 million registered voters in the region, noting that active participation remained the strongest tool against electoral manipulation. It added that it was strengthening its structures at polling units and collation centres to ensure effective monitoring of the electoral process and lawful protection of votes from accreditation to the final declaration of results. The group also urged its members to remain vigilant, report suspicious electoral activities to relevant authorities and support peaceful, transparent and credible elections. KNN expressed optimism over what it described as increased political awareness among youths in the South-East, saying many previously disenchanted voters had renewed interest in the electoral process following the political alliance between former Anambra State Governor, Mr Peter Obi, and Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso. The group described the Obi/Kwankwaso alliance as “a watershed in Nigeria’s democratic journey,” saying it had restored hope among citizens who had become dissatisfied with the country’s political process. Reaffirming its commitment to the success of the alliance in the region, KNN reiterated its earlier pledge to deliver at least one million votes for the Obi/Kwankwaso ticket in each of the five South-East states during the 2027 presidential election. The group urged eligible voters in the South-East to emulate their counterparts in other regions by actively participating in the electoral process, stressing that political power can only be achieved through engagement. “Don’t be a bystander; prepare to participate actively in deciding the nation’s future through the ballot rather than apathy,” the statement added. The post 2027: Kwankwaso Group unveils strategy to curb vote buying, boost S’East turnout appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Breaking: Tinubu directs EFCC to vacate order freezing Osun Govt account
items.description: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has directed the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to immediately approach the court to vacate the order freezing the accounts of the Osun State Government. The President’s directive followed the controversy generated by the EFCC’s move to freeze the state government’s accounts, coming days before the Osun State governorship election. In a statement issued on Thursday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, President Tinubu said he was concerned about the timing of the action, noting that steps taken by federal institutions are often attributed to him as President, even when he may not have prior knowledge of such actions. The statement said the President was not embarrassed by the EFCC’s exercise of its mandate, backed by a court order, but by the timing of the action. “Since assuming office, I have consistently maintained that anti-corruption and law enforcement agencies must be allowed to discharge their statutory responsibilities independently, professionally, without fear or favour, or political interference,” Tinubu said. He stated that he had deliberately refrained from directing or interfering in the operational activities of the EFCC and other investigative or prosecutorial agencies because strong democratic institutions operating within the law are essential to good governance and the rule of law. According to the President, institutions of state have been established by law with clearly defined powers and must be allowed to function independently. Tinubu said although he was yet to be fully briefed on the facts that informed the EFCC’s decision to approach the court for the freezing order, he believed the timing of the action was inappropriate. “Osun State is only a few days away from its gubernatorial election. Therefore, nothing ought to be done to give an impression that the EFCC or indeed any other agency of the Federal Government is being used to interfere with the election,” he said. The President said he was compelled to intervene in the matter in the overriding public interest to preserve confidence in the integrity, credibility and fairness of the democratic process. “Accordingly, I have directed the EFCC to immediately proceed to the court to vacate the order and discontinue whatever action it has instituted against the Osun State Government in this regard,” Tinubu stated. items.title: How the new generation of left-wing US media is powering progressive candidates
items.description: Progressive candidates continue to rack up wins in primary elections across the United States, propelled by a new left-wing media ecosystem allowing them to build a national profile on their own terms — and sidestep the traditional gatekeepers of the Democratic establishment. For Pennsylvania state Representative Chris Rabb, a Democratic socialist who recently prevailed in a congressional primary against a more moderate rival, appearances on programs like “The Majority Report with Sam Seder” and “Breaking Points” played a key role in his political breakthrough. “It helps me increase my visibility, validation and ability to raise money,” said Rabb, describing it as “a Venn diagram of success”. This fast-growing world of left-wing websites, podcasters, YouTube hosts and livestreamers — many of whom blend opinion journalism and activism — affords candidates a sympathetic space to sharpen their message and mobilise grassroots support. But it also risks deepening the fissures in the Democratic Party, analysts say, and alienating moderates in the coalition. On Tuesday, progressive Abdul El-Sayed eked out a victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary against Haley Stevens, the preferred candidate of the party establishment. El-Sayed, a former state health official and a rising star in left-wing media, was massively outspent in television advertising — funded by tens of millions of dollars from pro-Israel and other outside groups — but still managed to win in a swing state carried by Republican President Donald Trump in 2024. New media entrepreneurs say they are filling a void in mainstream political coverage and providing a platform for candidates with views that have long been underrepresented in Washington. They include advocacy for universal healthcare, abolishing ICE and cutting off military aid to Israel. “There is an audience and a demand and a hunger for different viewpoints,” said Mehdi Hasan, a former MSNBC host who launched his own news organisation, Zeteo , in 2024. “The same energy that enabled us to be a success as a media entity has enabled a lot of political candidates to be successes.” A growing audience The American left has long had its own constellation of shows and publications. But as the reach of, and trust in, traditional media declines and consumers look elsewhere for news, independent content creators are becoming political kingmakers. While much smaller and less well-funded than right-wing media, the left’s growing network of podcasters, streamers and digital publishers is becoming an increasingly important force in Democratic politics, shaping primary campaigns, fundraising and activist organising. Zeteo has 700,000 Substack subscribers, up 50 per cent from a year ago. “The Majority Report with Sam Seder” has more than two million subscribers on YouTube and roughly 75pc of listeners are under age 55. Progressive commentator and activist Hasan Piker has more than three million followers on Twitch. For campaign strategists, the appeal of this new media environment is simple. Their candidates can have long, in-depth conversations on policy issues — the kind seldom seen on cable news — engage directly with voters and generate clips that can be blasted across social platforms. “I think we help create early enthusiasm,” said Sam Seder. “Our audience in particular has a lot of activists and a lot of people who run activist organisations, and I know we have a lot of legislative staffer types.” Candidates often move through the same circuit of shows and creators, allowing audiences to discover them through trusted ideological allies, said Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic operative and co-host of the political podcast “Nobody Knows Anything”. In turn, rising stars on the left help emerging media figures build their brands. “It’s interconnected,” said Hasan. “I don’t think one is necessarily leading the other.” ‘Preaching to the choir’ Most of the left-wing media personalities that have risen to prominence in recent years are unapologetic partisans. “Breaking Points” co-host Krystal Ball took part in a livestreamed August fundraiser for El-Sayed and other progressive candidates in Michigan. Piker canvassed last week for Francesca Hong, who is vying to be the first democratic socialist governor of Wisconsin, and took part in El-Sayed’s election night party in Detroit. “The work is only beginning,” he posted to X as the last votes trickled in on Tuesday night. Piker has voiced support for Hamas, used the word “cracker” to refer to white people and said that “America deserved 9/11,” a comment he later described as inappropriate. He did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. He has built a deeply devoted following on his daily Twitch streams, where he hosts free-floating discussions about hot-button issues — similar to Joe Rogan, the influential right-leaning podcaster who endorsed Trump in 2024. For Seder, the goal of “Majority Report” is less about persuading swing voters than educating and energising those already in their corner. “We may be preaching to the choir, but the choir is then going out and preaching to the independents,” he said. Hans Noel, a professor of government at Georgetown University, said these creators and outlets “energise voters who find the party’s platform too lukewarm or uninspiring.” “At the same time,” he added, “factional voices are not always interested in compromise,” which could pose a problem for candidates like El-Sayed as they seek to win over more moderate Democrats in the general election. An opposition party Jennifer Welch and Angie “Pumps” Sullivan, friends from Oklahoma City, started the “I’ve Had It” podcast in 2022 — a venue to vent about all the things that annoyed them, from the antics of reality stars to their own misbehaving children. It wasn’t until the 2024 presidential campaign that they began to talk about politics, savaging Trump in typically irreverent terms. Soon, they were interviewing Democratic presidential hopeful Kamala Harris and attending the party convention in Chicago. Their show now has more than 5.2 million subscribers and followers across YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. Listeners “are coming to us to get news and to get our opinion on the news”, Welch told Reuters . El-Sayed appeared on the podcast twice, and Welch endorsed him on-air, a decision she described as a “layup”. “I think that the Democratic base is so much further than what the establishment realises,” she said, “and I think candidates like Abdul are the future of the Democratic Party if we are to be an opposition party.”

items.title: Mahama assures helicopter crash families of continued national support one year on
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has assured the families of the eight victims of the August 6, 2025 military helicopter crash that the government and the people of Ghana remain united in supporting them as the nation commemorates the first anniversary of the tragedy. The assurance was given on Thursday, August 6, during a National Inter-Faith Memorial Service organised to honour the eight individuals who lost their lives when a Ghana Armed Forces Z-9 helicopter crashed while on an official assignment in the Adansi Akrofuom District of the Ashanti Region. President Mahama paid tribute to the victims, describing them as dedicated patriots whose commitment to national service would never be forgotten. He noted that although a year had passed since the incident, the pain and grief endured by their families remained profound. Addressing the bereaved families, the President acknowledged that no words could fully ease their sorrow but assured them that the nation continued to share in their grief. “To the bereaved families, permit me once again to convey the deepest condolences of the government and the people of Ghana. I know that no speech can erase your pain, no anniversary can fill that empty seat at your dining table, and no ceremonies can replace the voices that you long to hear. “You have borne your grief with remarkable courage and dignity, and in doing so, you have reminded all of us that love does not end with death; it endures in memory, faith and the lives we choose to live thereafter. “Please rest assured that the nation still mourns with you, and your loved ones did not die alone; they belong to all of Ghana, and we will continue to remember them.” The August 6, 2025 crash claimed the lives of eight people, including senior government officials and military personnel, and remains one of Ghana’s most devastating aviation disasters in recent history.

‘God has sustained us with strength and hope’ – Omane Boamah’s family reflects on year of grief
items.description: The family of the late Defence Minister, Dr Edward Kofi Omane Boamah, says it remains grateful to God for granting them strength, comfort and hope in the year since the military helicopter crash that claimed the lives of eight people. Speaking on behalf of the bereaved families during a national interfaith memorial service held on Thursday, August 6, family representative Charles Ohene Oti acknowledged that the past 12 months had been filled with profound grief but said faith had sustained them through the difficult period. “While the past year has been marked by deep grief and loss, God has sustained us with strength, comfort and hope,” he said. He noted that although the families continue to mourn the loss of their fathers, husbands, sons and brothers, they remain thankful for the lives they lived, the sacrifices they made and their dedicated service to Ghana. “Though we deeply miss our beloved fathers, husbands, sons and brothers, we remain grateful for the lives they lived, the service they rendered to Ghana, and the enduring legacies they left behind,” he added. Mr Ohene Oti also expressed appreciation to the Reverend Ministers, Imams and other religious leaders who have stood by the families with prayers, spiritual guidance and encouragement since the tragedy. “We are also grateful to the Reverend Ministers, Imams and all religious leaders leading today’s interfaith memorial service. Your prayers, spiritual guidance and support have been a source of comfort to our families throughout this difficult journey,” he stated. The memorial service was held to mark one year since the Ghana Armed Forces Z-9 helicopter crashed in the Adansi Akrofuom District of the Ashanti Region while travelling from Accra to Kumasi, killing all eight occupants on board. The victims included Dr Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed, Minister for Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation; Acting Deputy National Security Coordinator Alhaji Muniru Mohammed; former Ashanti Regional Minister Dr Samuel Sarpong; former NDC parliamentary candidate Samuel Aboagye; as well as three Ghana Armed Forces personnel — Squadron Leader Peter Bafemi Anala, Flying Officer Manaen Twum Ampadu and Sergeant Ernest Addo Mensah. The one-year remembrance brought together government officials, religious leaders, relatives of the deceased and members of the public to honour the victims and reflect on their contributions to national service.

items.description: Aug 6 (Reuters) - A 25-year-old Afghan man who rammed his car into a union rally in Munich last year, killing two people, has been given a life sentence, a German court said on Thursday. items.title: Transparency International calls for stronger reforms after survey reveals increased public bribery demands
items.description: Transparency International Ghana has urged targeted institutional reforms after a Ghana Statistical Service survey showed increased demands for bribes by public officials in 2025. The organisation said the findings should strengthen preventive measures, sanctions, and integrity systems across public institutions rather than discourage anti-corruption efforts. In an interview with the Ghana News Agency, Mary Addah, Executive Director of Transparency International Ghana, said the findings were consistent with the organisation’s long-standing concerns about bribery in the delivery of public services. “The report is not surprising for us at all. It confirms that there are systemic factors that continue to facilitate bribery, and those are what we need to address,” she said. The comments followed the release of the Ghana Statistical Service’s latest Governance Series survey, which found that public officials demanded bribes more frequently in 2025 than in the previous survey period. The report indicated that about seven in every 10 people who paid bribes said they were directly asked to do so by public officials. It also showed that although more Ghanaians refused to pay bribes, demands for unofficial payments increased across public institutions. Mrs Addah said the figures should not be interpreted as evidence that the fight against corruption had failed. “The important issue is to identify the gaps that promote bribery and implement measures that reduce those risks rather than conclude that nothing is working,” she said. Mrs Addah urged government institutions, particularly those frequently cited for bribery, to conduct corruption risk and vulnerability assessments and implement measures to address identified weaknesses. She also called for accelerated digitalisation of public services to reduce direct contact between officials and citizens, saying fewer face-to-face interactions would minimise opportunities for bribery. Mrs Addah advocated strict enforcement of institutional codes of conduct, stronger integrity and ethics education, and consistent sanctions against officials found engaging in corrupt practices. The Governance Series survey forms part of Ghana’s monitoring of Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 16.5.1, which measures the proportion of people who had contact with public officials and paid or were asked to pay a bribe during the previous 12 months. It is expected to be conducted every six months to track trends in bribery and support evidence-based anti-corruption policies.

items.title: ‘We miss his wisdom and guidance’ – Muniru Limuna’s son pays tribute at memorial service
items.description: Late Alhaji Lumina Muniru’s son has paid an emotional tribute to his late father at the National Inter-Faith Memorial Service, describing his life as one defined by love, humility, service and integrity, and saying his values continue to guide the family and many people whose lives he touched. Speaking at the National Inter-Faith Memorial Service for the departed eight on August 6, Muniru’s son said the family’s grief began with disbelief as they struggled to come to terms with losing a cherished father, mentor and public servant. “One year ago, we stood before the nation in disbelief, struggling to find a way to say goodbye to our beloved son and father,” he said. He recalled how the family celebrated his remarkable life and remembered him as a loving husband, father, brother, mentor and a man whose presence inspired those around him. According to him, the past year has been a difficult journey as the family has learned to live without him. “Today, those words carry an even deeper meaning because for an entire year, we have had to learn what life looks like without him. The past year has changed us in ways we never imagined,” he said. Mr Muniu’s son said there have been many moments when the family wished they could hear his voice again, seek his advice on important decisions or simply spend time with him. He described missing his wisdom, reassurance and the love that kept the family together, but added that even in his absence, his legacy continues to provide direction. He said Alhaji Muhammad was not only a pillar of strength to the family but also a dedicated public servant and trusted colleague who served Ghana with compassion, humility and a strong sense of duty. “His life taught us that leadership is not measured by position but by service to others. He taught us that true strength is found in kindness, that leadership begins with listening, and that integrity is life’s greatest treasure,” he said. Alhaji’s son said those lessons remain a guiding principle for the family as they continue to honour his memory. He noted that one of the greatest comforts the family has found over the past year is hearing stories from people across the country about his kindness, generosity and compassion. “Through the way he lived, he gave us a family that extends far beyond our own,” he said. According to him, although the family lost a beloved member, Ghana also lost a remarkable servant whose contributions and character will continue to be remembered. He expressed appreciation to the President, the Government of Ghana, friends, extended family members and all Ghanaians who supported them throughout their period of grief. “Your prayers, your kindness, and your unwavering support have carried us through our darkest days,” he said. “Daddy, until we meet again, may you continue to rest in perfect peace.”

items.title: ‘No speech can erase your pain’ – Mahama consoles families of helicopter crash victims
items.description: President John Mahama has consoled the families of the eight state officials who died in the August 6, 2025, helicopter crash, acknowledging that no speech or ceremony can take away the pain of their loss. Speaking at the national inter-faith memorial service held in Accra on Thursday, August 6, to mark one year since the tragedy, President Mahama said the grief of losing loved ones cannot be fully addressed through words or public commemorations. “To the bereaved families, permit me to once again convey the deepest condolences of the government and people of Ghana. I know that no speech can erase your pain, no anniversary can fill that empty seat at your dining table, and no ceremonies can replace the voices that you long to hear or the embraces that you still miss,” he said. The President noted that the victims left behind families, dreams and unfinished responsibilities, but their contributions to Ghana’s development would continue to be remembered. He assured the families that the nation shares in their grief and will continue to honour the sacrifices of the eight individuals who lost their lives in service to the country. “Please rest assured that the nation still mourns with you. Your loved ones did not die alone; they belong to all of Ghana, and Ghana will continue to remember them,” he said. READ ALSO: Ghana’s Defence Minister, 7 others die in tragic helicopter crash The August 6, 2025 helicopter crash claimed the lives of Defence Minister Dr Edward Kofi Omane-Boamah, former Agriculture Minister Dr Ibrahim Murtala Mohammed and six others, including three Ghana Air Force crew members, while they were travelling to the Ashanti Region in connection with efforts to combat illegal mining.

items.title: Mahama urges recognition of public servants’ sacrifices as Ghana marks one year since helicopter crash
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on Ghanaians to appreciate and honour public servants while they are still serving, rather than waiting until tragedy strikes before recognising their sacrifices. Speaking at the National Inter-Faith Memorial Service held in Accra to mark one year since the military helicopter crash that claimed the lives of eight state officials and military personnel, President Mahama said many public servants make significant sacrifices that often go unnoticed. He said those who dedicate their lives to public service frequently endure difficult conditions, spend long periods away from their families and take risks because of their commitment to national development. “Much of their work goes unnoticed. They travel long distances. They spend countless hours away from their families. They endure difficult conditions. They make decisions under pressure. They accept risks because they believe that Ghana’s progress is worth every effort,” he said. The President said public servants play a critical role in protecting and advancing the country, but their efforts are often fully appreciated only after tragic events occur. “And too often we celebrate such service only after tragedy strikes,” he said. He urged Ghanaians to develop a culture of recognising dedication and sacrifice as public service is being performed daily. “Today we must resolve to appreciate public service even as it is performed daily. To appreciate those who labour faithfully, often without recognition, because they believe in something that is greater than themselves,” President Mahama added. Turning to the families of the eight victims of the helicopter crash, the President expressed condolences on behalf of the government and people of Ghana. “To the bereaved families, let me once again convey the deepest condolences of the government and people of Ghana,” he said. President Mahama acknowledged that no words or ceremony could completely remove the pain caused by the loss of their loved ones. “I know that no speech can erase your pain,” he said. The August 6, 2025 helicopter crash claimed the lives of Defence Minister Dr Edward Kofi Omane Boamah, Environment, Science and Technology Minister Dr Ibrahim Murtala Mohammed, security officials and Ghana Air Force personnel while they were travelling on official duty connected to efforts against illegal mining. The first anniversary memorial service brought together government officials, religious leaders, members of the diplomatic community, security personnel and families of the deceased to honour their lives and sacrifices.

items.title: La Guinée réclame à la France les crânes de l’Almamy Bokar Biro et de ses compagnons
items.description: Conakry a officiellement transmis à Paris une demande de restitution visant les restes mortels du dernier Almamy du Fouta-Djalon et de trois de ses proches, actuellement conservés au musée de l’Homme. La demande a été déposée le 27 juillet 2026, rapportent des médias. Cette démarche marque une nouvelle étape majeure dans la réappropriation par la Guinée de la mémoire de ses figures anticoloniales. Un nouveau chapitre s'ouvre dans la diplomatie culturelle entre la France et la Guinée. Ce jeudi 6 août 2026, la demande officielle de restitution des dépouilles de l'Almamy Bokar Biro, de son père, de son frère et de son chef de guerre fait la Une de plusieurs médias. La requête, formellement déposée le 27 juillet dernier auprès des autorités françaises, fait suite à une première initiative lancée mi-juillet pour récupérer les objets personnels d'une autre figure majeure de la résistance, Samory Touré. Dernier dirigeant de l'État théocratique du Fouta-Djalon (fondé en 1725), Bokar Biro s'est imposé à la fin du XIXe siècle comme un obstacle majeur à l'expansion coloniale française en Afrique de l'Ouest. Après sa décapitation, son crâne ainsi que ceux de ses proches avaient été rapportés en France comme des trophées de guerre, une pratique alors courante à l'époque coloniale. Comme l'a précisé, ce jeudi 6 août 2026 à l'antenne de RFI, le ministre guinéen de la Culture, Moussa Moïse Sylla, dont les déclarations ont largement été relayées par plusieurs médias, les recherches menées par la partie française ont permis de localiser avec précision ces vestiges historiques: «Depuis mi-juillet, nous avions déjà fait une autre demande à la France portant sur les objets personnels de l'Almamy Samory Touré et des recherches (…) ont été faites à notre demande au sujet du crâne de l'Almamy Bokar Biro Barry et de ses compagnons. C'est fin juillet que nous avons eu une réponse de la partie française, nous informant que ces crânes ont été retrouvés. Et donc nous avons fait la demande officielle de restitution». Cette démarche légale s'appuie directement sur le cadre juridique fixé en 2023 par le Parlement français concernant la restitution des restes humains issus des collections publiques. Pour orchestrer ce retour, les autorités guinéennes ont mis sur pied un comité scientifique. Elles espèrent aboutir à un rapatriement effectif d'ici un à deux ans. Pour le gouvernement guinéen, l'enjeu mémoriel est primordial. Reconnus comme des héros de la nation au même titre que les figures de la résistance en Basse-Guinée ou en Guinée forestière, Bokar Biro et ses compagnons doivent retrouver leur place dans la mémoire nationale. «Ce n'est pas quelqu'un d'anodin dont le crâne doit continuer à être exposé dans un musée en France», a affirmé Moussa Moïse Sylla, avant d'ajouter qu’«Aux côtés de l'Almamy Samory Touré et de héros que nous avons connus en Guinée forestière, en Basse-Guinée, l'Almamy Bokar Biro, en tant que dernier Almamy du Fouta-Djalon, est donc un héros». Revenant sur le contexte historique de cette exécution, Mohamed Amirou Conté, directeur du musée national de Guinée à Conakry et membre du comité scientifique, a rappelé l'engagement de l'ancien souverain: «Il était un farouche défenseur de la liberté, c'est pour ça qu'il a été décapité. Il a été décapité parce qu'il était contre la pénétration coloniale au Fouta». Cette procédure s'inscrit dans un mouvement plus large de restitutions accordées par la France, à l'instar des restes humains remis à l'Algérie en 2020 ou à Madagascar l'année dernière. Contrairement aux pratiques muséales occidentales, les dépouilles rapatriées de Paris ne seront toutefois pas exposées au public. Comme le soulignent les autorités culturelles à Conakry, les crânes feront l'objet d'une sépulture solennelle. «Exposer un crâne chez nous, ça ne se fait pas. Nous, les restes humains, on les enterre dignement. Mais les exposer dans un musée, ce n’est pas dans nos traditions et dans notre culture», soutient Mohamed Amirou Conté. Plus qu'une simple transaction administrative, le retour de ces dépouilles permettra enfin d'offrir à ces martyrs de la colonisation le repos et l'hommage sacré que commande la tradition guinéenne. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article La Guinée réclame à la France les crânes de l'Almamy Bokar Biro et de ses compagnons est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: UNDERSTANDING IRAN’S WAR STRATEGY
items.description: “And worse I may be yet. The worst is not So long as we can say, ‘This is the worst.’” — William Shakespeare, *King Lear* PROLOGUE The United States’ on-again, off-again war against Iran continues. While we are witnessing another lull at the time of writing, after a brief escalation following the signing of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), the structural logic of the conflict remains unchanged. If anything, Ukraine’s sinking of Iran’s merchant ship in the Caspian Sea threatens to imbricate the European and Asian theatres, especially if Kyiv attacks more Iranian ships and Iran retaliates. The war imposed on Iran by the US and its Zionist partner already involves 12 active state actors, a number that makes untangling the entanglement into a nightmare. Notwithstanding, many people in Pakistan have raised a number of questions regarding Iran’s policy and continue to fuss over why Iran can’t just cut a deal with the United States, get sanctions relief and get on with life. This article is an attempt to explain what guides Iran’s politico-strategic approach and how that affects Tehran’s operational strategy and its tactical responses, the three distinct but overlapping levels of war. The critics’ frustration is understandable. Pakistan is contiguous to Iran. Any internal and external shocks in that country affect it. Oil and gas and the entire ecosystem that impacts petrochemical industries and agriculture is Pakistan’s lifeline. Given Pakistan’s fragile economy, energy scarcity and price shocks have a direct and negative impact on the country. Pakistan also has friendly ties with the Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia. These states are in Iran’s crosshairs. That adds to Islamabad’s diplomatic and economic woes. It desperately wants an early end to the war, which is what informs its mediation efforts. Problem: the war is much bigger than Pakistan’s interests. With the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East and their escalation, many concerns have understandably been expressed in Pakistan about where the war is headed. Some have questioned Iran’s strategy and its steadfast refusal to come to a compromise with the United States on conditions dictated by the latter. What is Tehran’s endgame, they wonder. Ejaz Haider attempts to unpack the strategic logic that underpins Iran’s decisions… By now, Iran has been subjected to US perfidy four times: US President Donald Trump unilaterally scuppering a multilateral deal — the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action ( JCPOA ) — with Iran in 2018; the 2025 attacks, even as Iran was negotiating with the US; the repeat in 2026; and the US violation of clauses 1 and 5 of the MoU, which resulted in the latest round of fighting and escalation. Flagging this is important because the current line of questioning runs the risk of shifting the burden of war termination and making a deal from the aggressor (US) to the victim (Iran). That framing is problematic by all metrics and renders the methodology flawed a priori. An Iranian missile system is displayed in Azadi Square in Tehran, Iran, on July 30, 2026. — WANA via Reuters/File WHY IS IRAN NOT MAKING A DEAL? A counter question could be, is Iran playing solitaire? Expecting Tehran to make a deal without any reference to actions by the US, which imposed this war on Iran, is to either falsify all known facts or insinuate that Iran must accept the terms set by the aggressor — ie seek a deal without reference to why the US-Zionist duo started this war, what were/are their objectives, and what it means for Iran if they were to achieve those objectives. And for Iran to make such a deal for what? To avoid pain? Get rich? In an ideal world, avoiding pain is the best course of action. There is nothing bad about getting rich, either. Iran definitely wants to avoid pain and get rich if it means exploiting its full potential as a state and society with a very high literacy rate and impressive STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) achievements. But there’s a context here, of perpetual threat, and it requires that Iran, after having taken and absorbed much pain, must ensure that no external power can attack it in the future, whenever it so desires. Not ensuring that would mean squandering its current thin advantage, taking pain without any gains. That’s stupidity, not strategy. The central lesson of Iran’s history with the US, and more specifically with Trump, is simple: never make concessions on the basis of future promises. The operating principle, after being stung by Trump consistently, is zero trust and verifiable implementation. Those who say that Iran shouldn’t play hardball would do well to listen to what Oman’s foreign minister, Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi, told CBS News on February 27 about the concessions Iran had made. He stated that a nuclear deal with Iran was “within our reach”, ensuring that Iran would not accumulate nuclear material (zero stockpiling) and accept full verification. He said that Iran had gone beyond the 2015 JCPOA and stressed that there was no alternative to diplomacy. The interview took place in Washington, DC, shortly after Albusaidi had met with US Vice President J.D. Vance to conduct high-stakes diplomatic negotiations. By the early morning hours of February 28, the US-Zionist decapitation and degradation strikes had begun . So, yes, critics must forgive Iran if it is not entirely convinced of US-Zionist intentions and understands that talks have been a treacherous shield in preparation for war. Iran has no option but to take the hard path, a path not of its choosing but thrust on it by circumstances. While the US and the Zionist entity overlap quite a lot on Iran, it’s important to make a distinction: US wants Iran to surrender and be a subject state; Zionists want Iran destroyed as it stands today. The choice for Iran is not even about getting rich and losing sovereignty. It is about losing itself as a state. It has no choice but to stand up for its sovereignty and force the imperial power’s hand by raising the cost-exchange ratio for it. WON’T A COMPROMISE BE BETTER FOR IRAN’S ECONOMY? On that point about getting rich… Conflicts do not just happen one day. They have a structural-historical dynamic. They are also dictated by the interests of state parties, whether one is defending against an aggressor or has chosen to be the aggressor. The sense of history also defines how states and societies perceive themselves and their place in the world. This is not mere theoretical assumption. Take China. As a superpower today, its grand strategy merges historical pride with past trauma to drive its modern global ambitions. For millennia, China viewed itself as the Middle Kingdom, Zhngguó, centre of the world. The term reflected China’s ancient worldview, cultural pride, and geopolitical strategy. This status was shattered by the ‘Century of Humiliation’ (1839–1949), an era of Western and Japanese colonial exploitation, unequal treaties, and deep national subjugation. That century, as Sinologists agree, deeply informs China’s modern approaches. Iran too is a civilisational state. Much like China, its civilisational trajectory was violently disrupted and it was subjugated by foreign intervention — the humiliation and concessions of the 19th century; the CIA-MI6 coup of 1953; and the Iraq aggression of 1980 that lasted for eight years, with Baghdad being supported by Arab-Gulf states, the US and its European allies. Just as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) uses historical trauma to validate its rule, the Islamic Republic of Iran utilises this legacy as a core pillar of state ideology. The 1979 Islamic Revolution is officially framed as the moment Iran broke free from a century of colonial humiliation. There are multiple internal negatives of this policy in both states but that is outside the scope of this article. Realism, in both its classical and structural incarnations, offers empirical evidence that when security is scarce, a state cannot afford to care about perceived absolute gains in the future for two existential reasons: the peril of future intentions and the vulnerability of interdependence. With respect to the first, no state can ever truly know another state’s future intentions, a lesson Canada and European allies of the US are learning, forcing Canadian PM Mark Carney to talk about “the end of a pleasant fiction and the beginning of a harsh reality.” With respect to the second, chasing absolute gains usually requires deep economic or strategic cooperation. In a secure world, this liberal-internationalist approach — cooperation will make me wealthier and more secure than I was yesterday — is easier to answer and can also be hugely profitable. In a scarce-security environment, however, interdependence can create strategic vulnerabilities. If you rely on another state for your energy, technology or supply chains to achieve future gains, you have handed them a weapon. Realism demands strategic autonomy and self-reliance over future prosperity. This too is on full display through small-yard, high-fence strategies to kneecap adversaries by denying them access to tech, re-shoring, friend-shoring and domestic redundancies! Moreover, for Iran, Lockean cooperation has never been on offer; the demand is to surrender. The 2015 JCPOA, if it were allowed to continue, might have changed the dynamic, but Trump put paid to it. There’s another variable too when it comes to Iran: the Zionist serpent. While the US and the Zionist entity overlap quite a lot on Iran, it’s important to make a distinction: US wants Iran to surrender and be a subject state; Zionists want Iran destroyed as it stands today. There’s enough evidence of this emerging from Western sources and statements for me to belabour the point. The choice for Iran is not even about getting rich and losing sovereignty. It is about losing itself as a state. It has no choice but to stand up for its sovereignty and force the imperial power’s hand by raising the cost-exchange ratio for it. Before I put this point to rest, an example is in order: Gulf states are very rich; they attract a lot of global capital. And yet, not one is really sovereign; all are dependencies bowing to the very imperial power that’s waging war on Iran. At least two of them sleep happily in the Zionist bed despite the murderous, genocidal policies of the Zionists. A bulk carrier and an oil tanker sit anchored in Muscat, Oman, as the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed off: Iran understands that talks have been a treacherous shield in preparation for war by the US-Israel duo, which is why Iran is leveraging its control over the Strait of Hormuz | Reuters WHY DID IRAN ATTACK SHIPS AFTER SIGNING THE MOU? Many analysts in Pakistan blame Iran for this round of fighting. They argue that Iran should have looked at sanctions relief rather than insisting on controlling the Strait. Others have spoken about the illegality of collecting fees . Still others blame hardline elements within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) who presumably wanted to upstage the moderates and were not happy with the MoU. A few point to the four working groups and the High-Level Committee set up by the MoU and argue that Iran should have taken up the issue there. The issue of fees is controversial. But so far, Iran has not charged any fees, as per the MoU. The working groups had not begun functioning because Iran was involved in the state funeral of Syed Ali Khamenei . The US found the opportunity to push ships through the southern route. Missing the point leads to a flawed causal chain. The analyses adopt a geopolitical frame that views the US navy as a default, passive guarantor of global commons. That’s just not true and blinds them to how that action will act as a catalyst in regional escalation in this case. By starting the timeline only at the moment Iran fired at the ships, they exclude the compounding variable (the US naval escort deployment). With this boundary setting, they choose to analyse the “action” (the attack) while systematically omitting the “antecedent” (the escort policy). A proper methodology would require mapping all structural inputs that led to Iran’s action. The US escorting of ships is not a neutral act. It signals a provocative, forward military posture in Iran’s backyard. A robust analysis requires a dialectical approach to recognise the security dilemma, where US projection of power and Iran’s encirclement anxieties constantly feed into each other. The real question to ask is this: why does Iran want to control the Strait and why does the US want to deny Iran that control? The MoU’s clause five is clear in its wording (by the way, talk about the MoU being loosely-worded is just that, post-facto talk): “Upon the signing of this MoU, the Islamic Republic of Iran will make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels, with no charge for 60 days only, from the Persian Gulf to the Sea of Oman, and vice versa. The traffic of commercial vessels will immediately start, and considering the need for removing the technical and military obstacles, and de-mining by the Islamic Republic of Iran, will be instated within 30 days. The Islamic Republic of Iran will conduct dialogue with the Sultanate of Oman, to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz, in discussions with other Persian Gulf Littoral States, in line with applicable international law and the sovereign rights of coastal states of the Strait of Hormuz.” There are three points here, two in bold letters and the third in italics. 1. Iran will make arrangements, with no charge for 60 days from the Persian Gulf to the Sea of Oman and vice versa. 2. Iran will conduct dialogue with Oman to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait. 3. Any such arrangement will be in line with applicable International Law and the sovereign rights of coastal states. The first clearly states that Iran will make arrangements (not the US); the first 60 days will be free. This links up with the second point: “to define the future administration and maritime services” in consultation with Oman. Implication: beyond 60 days, Iran and Oman will figure out the administration and maritime services. Corollary: after 60 days, there may be a fee and the routes will be coordinated with Oman and Iran. (Oman is already in consultation with Iran and has forwarded its proposal to Iran. What will become of it remains to be seen.) The afterthought that the clause does not refer to any particular route and, therefore, the US navy can escort ships through the southern route is shystering. The US was/is clearly attempting to dilute Iran’s control, in violation of what MoU’s relevant clause states. When an express power or duty is given, the law implies the concurrent assignment of the necessary powers to execute it. The post-facto interpretation by the US contravenes the principle of good faith. WHY HASN’T IRAN ATTACKED THE ZIONIST ENTITY? Iran has not attacked the Zionists in this round because the Zionists have stayed away, embroiled as Benjamin Netanyahu is in the upcoming October polls and on the northern front against Hezbollah. Iran does not have unlimited resources. Any sensible planning requires that it husband its war-fighting capability. Hezbollah is keeping the Zionist entity busy at this stage. Internally, Netanyahu is being challenged effectively. As for targeting the Gulf states and Jordan, it’s somewhat amazing that this point is raised, given how deeply these states are interlocked with US interests. But there’s another reason too, as noted by some former US military officers, including Lt Gen Mark Hertling. Hertling identified Jordan’s Muwaffaq Salti Air Base as the largest concentration of advanced US airpower in the Middle East, housing F-35s, F-15Es, A-10s, and critical air defence networks like THAAD. He explained that the base is vital for projecting power against Iran while enabling “strategic plausible deniability” for Jordan. That hasn’t worked, as is clear from Iran’s strikes targeting early warning and radars. Jordan has been critical in shielding the Zionist entity from incoming Iranian missiles and drones. This is why Iran targeted and destroyed a $300 million AN/TPY-2 Forward Based X-band Transportable Radar operated by the US Army at the base, rendering the THAAD battery effectively blind. Iran has done this to US electronic warfare and radar systems elsewhere too. This makes the space for it to target the Zionists more effectively when it needs to do so. IS IRAN OVERPLAYING ITS HAND? This is an interesting question and subtly contains in it other questions! It is also grounded in some nuance. Military theorist Carl von Clausewitz spoke of the “culminating point of victory”, the point that denotes the critical threshold where military gains peak and begin to reverse into a disadvantage if pushed further. History offers many examples of this overreach. But this point is not on a metered scale; the buzzer doesn’t go off for the commander when gains reach that point. It is a judgement call. A commander has to work through and analyse multiple variables to figure out where and when to stop. I believe that while Iran must remain cognisant of this, the situation needs to be contextualised. The war has led to pain on both sides and a stalemate. Neither side has been defeated or has won in the classical sense. And while Iran has so far denied the US its strategic objective of bending Tehran to its will and fracturing it, the contest is on and Iran simply cannot let its guard down until the US realises that gambling for resurrection is resulting in increasingly diminishing returns. I have already discussed the structural logic of Hormuz above so I don’t need to repeat it. The essential point is that, in this contest, Iran is defending and reacting. Its victory lies in denial strategies. But yes, it has to be careful about figuring out the balance. The Strait is central to its strategy, sure. But what kind of balance can be struck, and as early as possible, is a vital question. Iran also has to signal to the Gulf states that its attacks have a context and, outside of that context, it seeks cooperation with them, not just because of geographic contiguity but also historical, cultural and trade ties. The most notable example is the backchannel between the UAE and Iran. It’s going to be a frosty peace; the UAE will use this as part of a suite of strategies. But pragmatism could work for both sides. This is also applicable to other Gulf states. American President Donald Trump signs the US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MoU) at the Palace of Versailles in France on June 17, 2026: Trump reneged on the MoU by violating its clauses regarding Lebanon and Strait of Hormuz | White House WON’T IRAN BRINGING ANSAR ALLAH INTO THE FIGHT BRING KSA AND UAE TOGETHER? This question takes it for granted that Yemen’s Ansar Allah (Houthis is the wrong shorthand for the movement’s name) operates purely at the behest of Iran. As multiple analyses suggest, Ansar Allah, while a strong ally of Iran, primarily operates within the Yemeni context. Recent analytical and investigative reports present a nuanced picture that goes beyond the narrative of Ansar Allah being an Iranian puppet. The current escalation was sparked on July 13, when Yemen’s Aden-based Internationally Recognised Government (IRG) bombed the runway at Sanaa International Airport, preventing an Iranian plane from landing. The plane carried an Ansar Allah delegation that had travelled to Iran for Ayatollah Khamenei’s funeral. The strike shattered a fragile, unwritten four-year truce between the Saudi-led coalition and Ansar Allah. Regional reports underscore that Ansar Allah operates primarily on its own local calculations rather than acting purely on Iranian command. In fact, it is far more independent than the IRG, which is an extension of Riyadh. The group’s decision to transition from targeting global shipping to a direct, localised “siege-for-siege” blockade on Saudi Arabia is driven by local dynamics, including economic stress. The group is facing domestic strain over a longstanding financial stalemate with the Aden government. Framing their actions as a defence of Yemeni sovereignty against external blockades, Ansar Allah uses the escalation to rally mass public support domestically. Their military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, explicitly framed the missile strikes on Saudi oil hubs such as Yanbu as local retaliation for airspace violations. While Ansar Allah has its own domestic drivers, there’s no gainsaying that the crisis serves Iran’s broader geopolitical goals. The blockade on Saudi shipping allows Tehran to project power and threaten global energy corridors without engaging in a direct state-on-state conventional war. Within the Yemeni context, neither the IRG nor Ansar Allah is looking for a return to full-scale war. In the broader context, Iran’s offer to mediate between Ansar Allah and Riyadh is a signal that Tehran does not want it to escalate. The essential point is that, given the complexity of the actors involved and their varied interests, all sides are attempting to create a balance between the pressures of the immediate and the long-term reconfiguration of the Gulf and the Middle East. As for bringing Riyadh and Abu Dhabi together, they will come together on certain issues while remaining apart on others because of structural reasons. EPILOGUE There are three sets of actors in this war: the United States and the Zionist entity (the latter operates with and also independent of the US); the Gulf states, Jordan and Egypt; and Iran and its regional allies (the ‘Axis of Resistance’). There are also differences within the Gulf set but we will not press that point here. Each set has its objectives. The US has been the primary force in the Greater Middle East since World War II; the Zionists act as its outpost. Jordan and Egypt are US dependencies and have peace treaties with the Zionist entity. The Gulf set, excluding Saudi Arabia, comprises tiny states with oil wealth in varying degrees. These states, most notably the UAE, have tried to compensate for their geographic and demographic weaknesses by allying with the US and modernising their militaries within a capital/tech-intensive model. They are also, with varying degrees of success, trying to diversify their economies, investing abroad and attracting investments at home. The model requires peace and security. Iran is under sanctions since 1979. Its attempts to break out of isolation have repeatedly failed. During the Iran-Iraq War, the Gulf states, the US and its European partners fully backed Iraq. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) was birthed for the very purpose of containing Iran. Iran’s allies, non-state actors, are labelled “terrorist”. Its state ally, Syria, is now controlled by a former ‘Islamic State’/Al Qaeda leader, newly-minted and koshered by the West because he serves a purpose. Iran wants to secure itself. The US/Israel want to destroy it. The Gulf states want the US to defang Iran. These objectives create their respective incentive structures. They also impact Iran’s tactical, operational and political-strategic approaches. This is a very sketchy overview, of course. But the point is that analyses have to bring in multiple factors to figure out the dynamics at play. The situation is far too complex for linear causalities. In the end, however, the world remains anarchic. The US is waning but it still remains the strongest power. It never allowed itself to be subjected by laws and norms but Trump has expressed his disdain for norms and laws openly, even bragged about it. In the wolf world, one is reminded of King Lear’s eldest daughter Goneril’s cynical question in Shakespeare’s play, after her villainy is exposed: “Say, if I do, the laws are mine, not thine. Who can arraign me for’t?” The writer is a journalist interested in security and foreign policies. items.title: Call for Applications: Professional Translation Services (English ↔ French)
items.description: The Institute for Peace and Security Studies (IPSS) at Addis Ababa University invites applications from qualified individual translators and translation firms to provide on-call professional translation services (English ↔ French) during the period 24 August to 31 December 2026. The selected translator(s) or firm(s) will be engaged on an as-needed basis to support the translation of institutional, academic, and policy-related documents. Selection under this call does not guarantee a minimum volume of work. Qualifications Applicants should meet the following requirements: Minimum of four (4) years of proven professional translation experience, preferably in academic, policy, or international development settings; Native or near-native proficiency in both English and French; Strong knowledge of terminology related to peace, security, governance, development, and international affairs; Demonstrated ability to deliver accurate, high-quality translations within agreed deadlines; Excellent writing, proofreading, and attention to detail. Scope of Work The selected translator(s) and/or firm(s) will provide translation, editing, proofreading, and quality assurance services for a range of IPSS materials, including: Research publications and reports Policy briefs and concept notes Press releases and communication materials Training manuals and workshop materials Event and conference documents Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs), agreements, and official correspondence Meeting minutes Other institutional documents, as required Application Requirements Interested applicants are requested to submit: A current CV (for individual applicants) or company profile (for firms) highlighting relevant experience. Samples of previous translation work, where available. A financial proposal indicating professional rates (per word, per page, or per document, as applicable), clearly specifying the English ↔ French language pair. Estimated turnaround times for translation assignments. Contact details for at least two professional references. Selection Process Applications will be reviewed based on the applicants’ qualifications, relevant experience, quality of previous work, and financial proposal. IPSS reserves the right to select one or more individual translators and/or translation firms under this call. Submission Applications should be submitted to application@ipss-addis.org no later than 13 August 2026, 5:00 p.m. (EAT) with the subject line: Application – Professional Translation Services (English ↔ French) Only shortlisted applicants will be contacted. items.title: Agoè-Nyivé : Atopani, le tam-tam parlant qui perpétue l’héritage culturel de Togblékopé
items.description: Agoè-Nyivé, 6 août (ATOP) – La cour royale du chef canton de Togblékopé dans la commune Agoè-Nyivé 4 a vibré au son du tam-tam « Atopani » le jeudi 6 août. Sa résonance a donné le ton aux grandes cérémonies traditionnelles de libation et d’invocation des mânes des ancêtres pour le bon déroulement de la fête qui prendra fin le 15 août. Le tam-tam parlant demeure un puissant symbole de communication, d’autorité et de spiritualité dans ces communautés. Il rappelle l’attachement des populations du grand Lomé à leur riche patrimoine culturel Le détenteur du tam-tam Atopani, Kpodo-Drah Vioto, a souligné que la sortie de ce tam-tam annonce le début des festivités de l’édition 2026 de la fête Dunenyo za. Le chef du canton de Togblékopé, Togbuigan Kpodo-Drah Victor, a rappelé qu’Atopani constitue un héritage précieux transmis de génération en génération. Il a exhorté les jeunes à préserver cette richesse culturelle, symbole de l’identité, de l’histoire et des valeurs du peuple de Togblékopé. Des prières musulmanes, des activités sportives, des formations, des séances de reboisement et plusieurs activités culturelles sont au programme de cette édition. ATOP/ ASA/HKM

items.description: The Institute for Peace and Security Studies (IPSS) at Addis Ababa University invites applications from qualified individual interpreters and interpretation firms to provide on-call professional interpretation services in the following languages: English, Amharic, Arabic, French, and Portuguese from 24 August to 31 December 2026. The selected interpreter(s) or firm(s) will be engaged on an as-needed basis to provide simultaneous and/or consecutive interpretation during conferences, workshops, meetings, training sessions, and other institutional events. Selection under this call does not guarantee a minimum volume of work. Qualifications Applicants should meet the following requirements: Minimum of four (4) years of proven professional interpretation experience, preferably in academic, policy, diplomatic, or international development settings; Native or near-native proficiency in at least two of the following languages: English, Amharic, Arabic, French, and Portuguese, with demonstrated professional interpretation experience in the language combination(s) offered; Demonstrated experience providing simultaneous and/or consecutive interpretation for conferences, workshops, meetings, or similar events; Strong knowledge of terminology related to peace, security, governance, development, diplomacy, and international affairs; Demonstrated ability to deliver accurate, impartial, and high-quality interpretation while maintaining confidentiality and professional ethics; Excellent communication, listening, and interpersonal skills. Scope of Work The selected interpreter(s) or firm(s) will provide simultaneous and/or consecutive interpretation services for a range of IPSS activities, including: High-level conferences and forums; Workshops and training sessions; Policy dialogues and stakeholder consultations; Official meetings and roundtable discussions; Public lectures and panel discussions; Bilateral and multilateral engagements; Virtual and hybrid meetings, where required; Other institutional events, as required. Assignments may involve simultaneous, consecutive, or remote interpretation, depending on the nature and requirements of the event. Interpretation firms may also be requested to provide interpretation equipment and technical support, where applicable. Application Requirements Interested applicants are requested to submit: A current CV (for individual applicants) or company profile (for firms) highlighting relevant experience; A list of previous interpretation assignments, preferably for academic institutions, international organizations, government agencies, or conferences; A financial proposal indicating daily and/or hourly rates for simultaneous, consecutive, and remote interpretation services, where applicable, clearly specifying the language combination(s) offered; Availability and estimated response time for assignments; Contact details for at least two professional references. Selection Process Applications will be reviewed based on the applicants’ qualifications, relevant experience, previous interpretation assignments, language proficiency, and financial proposal. IPSS reserves the right to select one or more individual interpreters and/or interpretation firms under this call. items.title: Toubacouta : quand l’ostréiculture redonne vie et sourire
items.description: Imaginons un plat de « ceebu guédj » – symbole d’une alchimie entre la terre et l’océan – dépourvu de « toufeu » et de « pagne », fruits de mer incontournables, pour l’agrémenter. Heureusement, au Sénégal, les ostréicultrices nous sauvent d’un tel manquement. Mais, au-delà d’un simple acte de préservation gastronomique, c’est pour des raisons économiques que ces femmes s’enfoncent, chaque jour, dans les mangroves vaseuses du Sine-Saloum. Grâce à l’ostréiculture, elles maintiennent leurs foyers à flot et assurent la scolarité de leurs enfants. Pour la célébration de l’Année internationale des femmes agricultrices, l’Organisation des Nations unies pour l'alimentation et l'agriculture (FAO) a mis en lumière la contribution des femmes à l’économie à tous les niveaux. Une attention particulière a été accordée au secteur de l’ostréiculture dans la commune de Toubacouta. Sous un soleil pas du tout clément de cette matinée du 14 juillet 2026, les femmes du village de Nema Bah (Toubacouta) exposent le fruit de leur labeur. Sur la berge de la mangrove, témoin de leur peine et de leur abnégation, elles nous expliquent les secrets de l’ostréiculture, mais aussi son impact à la fois économique et social. Gagne Siri Sarr, membre du GIE « Yonn Dioffor », est exposante de fruits de mer : crevettes, huîtres, moules, coques, palourdes… tout y passe… Imprégnée de sueur, elle se montre très fière de son travail. Sa table force une pensée respectueuse envers les mets locaux comme le « soupou kandja », le « ceebu guédj » ou encore le « c’est bon ». D’excellents mets qui n’existeraient probablement pas sans les mains calleuses de dignes femmes à l’instar de Gagne Siri Sarr. Oui, l’ostréiculture est un travail fastidieux, en témoignent les stigmates sur les mains de celles et ceux qui la pratiquent. « C’est un métier difficile certes, mais c’est grâce à l’ostréiculture que nous tenons debout. Nous en tirons des bénéfices qui nous permettent d’assurer les frais de scolarité de nos enfants et de seconder nos époux pour subvenir aux besoins de toute la famille », explique Mme Sarr. Elle n’a pas manqué de saluer les efforts déployés par la FAO pour justement améliorer les conditions de travail de ces camarades ostréicultrices. À travers du matériel et des formations sur les méthodes de production et de commercialisation, la FAO, renseigne Gagne Siri Sarr, les initie à travailler plus efficacement et avec moins de peine. La mangrove, gage de stabilité socioéconomique Dans le village de Nema Bah, la mangrove est une manne nourricière d’une importance capitale. Conscientes de son importance, des femmes de la localité se sont regroupées autour du Gie « Yonn Dioffor » pour une pratique plus moderne et plus responsable. Selon Seynabou Diatta, présidente dudit groupement qui réunit les femmes ostréicultrices, leur activité joue un rôle essentiel dans l’économie, mais également dans la santé des populations locales. En effet, explique-t-elle, les produits issus de la mangrove leur permettent de nourrir leur famille avec des aliments riches en protéines et 100 % naturels. Mme Diatta insiste, en outre, sur la diversité des produits qui sont obtenus grâce à la mangrove, leur permettant d’avoir une alimentation diversifiée. À cela s’ajoute le rôle de la mangrove dans l’approvisionnement de la région naturelle du Sine-Saloum, voire du Sénégal, en produits halieutiques. Ainsi, la mangrove constitue pour elles la ressource financière la plus importante qu’il faut impérativement préserver. C’est d’ailleurs dans ce cadre qu’intervient le programme de valorisation du potentiel de la pêche et de l’aquaculture en Afrique, dans les Caraïbes et le Pacifique (FishH4Acp). Seynabou Diatta explique que sur le plan des ventes, ce projet a permis de raccourcir le temps de production, de réduire les pertes, d’améliorer la qualité des huîtres et, naturellement, d’enregistrer de meilleures performances financières. A lire aussi : Delta du Saloum : A la rencontre des maîtres de la traversée à Toubacouta « Grâce à l’appui de la FAO, à travers le programme Fish4ACP, nos produits sont de meilleure qualité. Nous avons appris des techniques qui nous permettent d’avoir des huîtres plus savoureuses et plus propres en six mois. Avant, les huîtres s'accrochaient beaucoup plus bas, au ras du sol vaseux de la mangrove. Par conséquent, il arrivait fréquemment que nous nous retrouvions avec des coquillages remplis de sable. Maintenant, elles sont placées beaucoup plus en hauteur. Et c’est cela qui nous permet d’obtenir des produits faciles à traiter et à transformer. Nos ventes ont connu un bond de plus de 80 % », dit Mme Diatta. D’ailleurs, elle explique que cette technique a donné un coup de pouce aux ventes et une meilleure réputation aux huîtres issues de la mangrove de Nema Bah. Toutefois, l’exposante estime qu’il reste encore à faire. Elle pense que la croissance de la production ostréicole doit être associée à une plus vaste stratégie commerciale. Seynabou Diatta plaide donc pour la labellisation des huîtres de Toubacouta, car elle veut aller à la conquête du monde. Et il y a de quoi partir à la conquête du marché international au regard des progrès techniques enregistrés. En effet, selon Amy Collé Gaye, administratrice nationale du programme Fish4ACP, le Sénégal peut valablement compter parmi les géants mondiaux de l’ostréiculture. Par sa position géographique et son ensoleillement, le Sénégal a un délai de production très court comparativement à des pays comme la France, dont le cycle de production est compris entre un an et deux ans. « Nous avons la chance d'avoir des mangroves qui sont riches en nutriment ; nous avons le soleil et les températures idéales pour produire des huîtres en un an tout au plus », explique l’experte halieutique. Et c’est justement pour cette raison que Seynabou Diatta, présidente du Gie Yonn Dioffor, milite pour la labellisation des huîtres du pays, avec notamment un bon branding, pour que le Sénégal puisse occuper sa place sur le marché mondial de l’ostréiculture. Par Assane FALL
