items.title: The Academics Who Caught Fire
items.description: Separating facts from lies, and real thoughts from fabrications, can seem more difficult than ever: Words and images are easily faked, and some writers at every stage—students, academics, novelists—are letting machines do the work for them. The author may as well be dead. Ubiquitous cameras are eroding human privacy , creating the sense that we live in a panopticon. And across many popular platforms, information is often shorn of context, if not outright false . The fact that I feed my kids and pay my rent as a novelist and teacher likely intensifies the queasiness I feel at these developments. Yet my profession also helps me understand that the idea of society coming apart might be the oldest story in the world. In the second half of the previous century, a group of mostly French theorists made this kind of instability their main subject. Systems built by humans were overpowering our ability to make choices, they explained. Society and language, the scaffolding on which our reality was built, were made up and farcical. I read these guys—mostly guys, often grouped together as structuralists and post-structuralists—in college, and they baffled and entranced me. After a mediocre high-school education spent checking boxes, the thrill of thinking , of elbowing my way through something hard and complicated, felt like coming to life. Trudging doggedly through these difficult, abstruse ideas—roughly 67 percent of which I felt sure I didn’t understand—made the world feel sharper, different. Twenty years later, looking back on their (not inaccurate) cultural diagnoses generates a complicated feeling: I’m reminded of that seductive sensation of stretching one’s brain, even as I hear speculation that artificial intelligence might one day make thinking obsolete. No book better captures this paradox than The Frenchmen , Emily Eakin’s new book about her encounters with post-structuralist ideas. Eakin entered college as an aspiring academic, but went on to spend her adult life in journalism (she is an editor at The New York Times ). Yet despite her experience in two unstable fields, and her focus on thinkers who proclaimed, among other things, “the death of the author,” her book is filled with life. Every page contains evidence of deep research, an eye for telling details, and the pleasure that can comes from sprawling, sometimes consternating thought. The Frenchmen opens as a sort of intellectual bildungsroman: At Harvard in the late 1980s—and especially in the classrooms to which Eakin gravitated as an undergraduate—French theory was the rage. It seemed both exclusive and rebellious. The protests of the ’60s seemed to be a distant memory, Ronald Reagan was president, and large portions of the population were quietly ignoring the thousands of deaths caused by AIDS. “In an era of complacency and self-satisfaction,” she writes, “theory was a symbol, however small, of intellectual nonconformism, a badge, like a pink mohawk, that marked you as a member of the counterculture, different from—and critical of—the docile horde.” Like so many college kids before her, Eakin, the child of two English-Ph.D. holders from Indiana, came to campus feeling ineffectual and small. The spirit of the times only amplified that impression, but the sheer force and seeming certainty of these fashionable thinkers gave her a sense of power. [ Read: The theory that explains Trump’s UFC fight ] Before long, Eakin comes to the titular French writers : Jacques Lacan (1901–81), Roland Barthes (1915–80), Louis Althusser (1918–90), Paul de Man (1919–83), Gilles Deleuze (1925–95), Michel Foucault (1926–84), Félix Guattari (1930–92), and Jacques Derrida (1930–2004). I gave you the dates of their lives because, in Eakin’s telling, they really matter. Having led the reader into their ideas through her own experience, she illustrates how impossible it is to separate any individual thinker’s theories or discoveries from the time in which they lived. This seems obvious, maybe, but in fact it contradicts these philosophers’ core belief in the irrelevance of biography. And to the extent that our lives often feel disembodied today—so much time spent staring at screens—Eakin’s approach is not just a refreshing way of explaining ideas, but also a reminder to readers that we are physical beings first. One of the primary tenets of most of the Frenchmen was that facts and meaning were difficult to pin down. There was only the text, over which the writer had little control. Even the self was ultimately an unstable text. “Within the structuralist framework,” Eakin explains, “an author was held to be of little account, a ‘fiction’ perpetrated by the ‘linguistic system,’ so it was easy to ignore the philosopher” and instead “focus exclusively on his words.” Eakin’s goal is the opposite: “to re-embody these men—to recover the hidden human element beneath their often stringent antihumanism.” In carefully parsing not only these men’s arguments but also their lives, Eakin is able to seduce us with their ideas. And by whipping back and forth between theory and life, documenting spats among the players, and jumbling timelines, she lets readers glimpse the twisty paths these ideas followed, the historical currents that accelerated their spread, and the way they still thrum through our lives. We spend the early chapters with the adolescent Eakin, for whom theory’s appeal was as much aesthetic—scarves and cigarettes, jeans with neckties—as it was intellectual. Eakin spent weeks imagining herself performing as Nadja, the wanton and elusive love interest from André Breton ’s semi-autobiographical novel of the same name. “I didn’t know what I wanted to be,” she writes. “I was hung up on something more basic: what it meant to be. I lacked confidence and, more to the point, skepticism. I didn’t know how to take theory in small doses.” This infatuation seemed to acquire the quality of an addiction. “Theory made thinking feel like doing . There was a rigor and beauty to it, an athletic strenuousness.” A combination of theoretical gloss, intellectual memoir, and group biography, The Frenchmen is never wholly any of the three, and this is both its great strength and the reason that it sometimes loses hold of itself. From Eakin’s early college days, readers move through various philosophies without the confusion and doubling back that reading the actual works frequently entails. We start with Sartre, Marx, and Freud, who give way to Althusser and Lacan. Nearly all of the structuralists thought Sartre’s emphasis on individual agency was absurd in the face of Vietnam, inequality, and the Cold War. People had no power after all; their unconscious, shaped by systems and structures, was actually in charge. [ Read: I will read Ulysses yes ] Such a smooth summary inevitably sacrifices complexity. My own descriptions have already shortchanged everyone I’ve mentioned. But Eakin doesn’t mean to untangle every theory, only to find “the hidden human element” that unites and explains the movement. Over and over, she knocks these philosophers’ experiences up against their thinking, lets us see these men move (sometimes awkwardly, sometimes dashingly) through time and space, and helps us understand how their theories reflected their lives. How, for instance, does your understanding of Foucault’s theory of power —that society is a trap constructed to discipline and punish—change when you know that he was told by his headmaster that he had to fix his homosexuality if he wanted to stay at school? What might Derrida’s famous notion of différance —that words and signs mean something only in relation to other words and signs—have to do with the fact that he was a French Algerian Jew, expelled from primary school because of his ethnicity? Sartre and Althusser, each fixated on the limits of freedom, had both been prisoners of war and struggled to reintegrate into civilian life. Both Deleuze and Barthes were not admitted to L’École Normale, which was considered one of the best schools in Paris, for different reasons; each went on to defy academic orthodoxy. Foucault was hospitalized after a suicide attempt; then he dropped acid in Death Valley. Althusser was diagnosed as bipolar, endured shock treatment, and eventually strangled his wife. Derrida was arrested (erroneously) for drug trafficking in Prague; Barthes was struck and killed by a laundry van. Nearly all the Frenchmen were fast drivers and sharp dressers. None of this made them structuralists or post-structuralists, but all of it is fairly extraordinary. Watching these details accrue leads to conclusions that undermine the doctrines of the Frenchmen: How could biography not be important? And also, how much more fascinating does it make these ideas? Unstable or not, the author is most certainly a text worth talking about. Instead of ideas bestowed by gods, these iconoclastic theories come to look like intellectual insurrections with both global and highly proximate causes. The eruptions of the 20th century, refracted through idiosyncratic, brilliant, sometimes troubled men, engendered new ways of thinking about freedom, collectivity, social control, and artistic creation. In Eakin’s account, you begin to see the alchemy through which these notions caught fire and spread. By the time Derrida died, in 2004, the fever of post-structuralism had long broken in the universities—and in Eakin’s mind. In the end, close reading didn’t lead to revolution. The students supposedly radicalized by Marxist theory and its descendants did not slow down the global march toward free markets and political triangulation. In the late ’80s, De Man was revealed to have been a Nazi apologist with a secret family stashed in Europe. Eakin, for her part, dropped out of her Ph.D. program and went on to work at the academic magazine Lingua Franca ; she was there when the outlet published an article by the NYU professor Alan Sokal , who revealed that he had duped a journal into publishing a hoax that mocked literary theory. The death knell of the Frenchmen had been rung before the end of the 20th century. [ Read: A bizarre, challenging book more people should read ] When Eakin, by 2004 already at the Times , was asked to read the paper’s prepared obituary for Derrida , she realized how thoroughly these once-vaunted men had been struck down. She laments the article’s “tone of condescension,” its emphasis on how “unintelligible” theory is: “The Times ’s Derrida was a caricature I recognized, and it seemed pointless, maybe even pretentious, to object.” Eakin now seems to regret her failure to ask for changes to the obituary, but she mentions extenuating circumstances that most anyone could understand. She was on maternity leave, and she was unsure what difference she could make. I also got the sense that she was deep inside a bureaucratic system whose rules she had learned to accept. But she wonders, years later, if she wrote off theory too easily—or too early. Maybe it seemed dead only because its influence was so diffuse. Its ideas were nowhere—and in evidence everywhere. Today, when the slipperiness of truth, the ubiquity of surveillance, and the pervasive politics of identity are all self-evident, an intellectual history of deconstruction seems less like a dip into the past than a sharper lens through which to view our present. Eakin’s skill in distilling and then weaving these ideas together within a biographical context not only gives them new life; it also supports her argument that these lives are essential to the work. The Frenchmen immerses the reader in the thinking and feeling of the world that came before it, and it explains, through one particular writer’s experience, the world we live in now.

items.title: La commune Tchaoudjo 2 lance l’élaboration de son PDC
items.description: Sokodé, 6 août (ATOP) – La commune Tchaoudjo 2 a amorcé, officiellement, le processus d’élaboration de son Plan de développement communal (PDC) lors d’un atelier réunissant les parties prenantes le mercredi 5 août à Lama-Téssi. Le PDC servira de boussole pour le développement communal sur une période de 5 ans, visant le bien-être social, économique, culturel, spatial et le développement harmonieux durable et résilient de la commune. Il permettra de faire de la commune Tchaoudjo 2, un exemple inspirant de planification territoriale intégrée, conciliant développement économique et préservation de l’environnement. Le document sera élaboré grâce à l’appui du programme « Restauration des paysages forestiers et bonne gouvernance dans le secteur forestier » (Forests4furure). Ce programme est cofinancé par l’Allemagne et le Luxembourg et mis en œuvre par la GIZ. L’élaboration de ce document s’appuiera sur un processus structuré permettant d’identifier les besoins réels des habitants, de concevoir des projets adaptés et de déterminer les sources de financement nécessaires à sa mise en œuvre. Afin d’assurer une prise en compte exhaustive des attentes locales, les citoyens seront consultés à chaque étape du projet. Le travail s’organisera en cinq phases, chacune comportant plusieurs étapes méthodologiques. Ces phases portent sur la préparation, la définition de la vision, des orientations stratégiques, des objectifs et des résultats attendus. Elles incluent également la programmation, la rédaction et la validation du plan puis son adoption par le Conseil municipal et son approbation par le préfet. Au cours de l’atelier, les parties prenantes ont suivi les grandes étapes du processus d’élaboration du PDC ainsi que la présentation des membres du comité de pilotage et du cabinet d’appui. Elles ont été éclairées sur le contexte de mise en œuvre du programme Forests4Future en lien avec la planification du développement. Le secrétaire général de la préfecture de Tchaoudjo, Bawo Moukadassi, l’administratrice des collectivités locales, Mme Pindra Samiya et le directeur régional de l’Environnement, Lt-Col Aledi Palakyèm ont invité chaque acteur à apporter sa contribution afin que le futur PDC de Tchaoudjo 2 reflète les aspirations des populations et constitue un référentiel pour les actions de développement des prochaines années. Le maire de la commune Tchaoudjo 2, Kiliou Kokolou a confirmé l’engagement de l’exécutif communal à accompagner et à œuvrer pour la bonne réussite de ce processus qui va définir la bonne trajectoire d’un développement inclusif et durable pour leur municipalité. Le conseiller technique de Forests4Future/GIZ, Dr Koumantiga Dabitora a réitéré l’engagement des partenaires à continuer d’accompagner le Togo dans ses efforts pour restaurer ses paysages forestiers, renforcer la gouvernance locale et améliorer les moyens de subsistance des populations. La rencontre a pris fin par une opération de mise en terre de plants. ATOP/MEK/JK/BV

Dunenyo Za 2026 : Des rites de libation annoncent la fête à Sagbado
items.description: Lomé, 6 août (ATOP) – Les autorités traditionnelles de Sagbado, dans la commune Golfe 7, ont organisé, une cérémonie de libation pour annoncer la célébration de la fête traditionnelle Dunenyo Za le jeudi 6 août au palais royal de Semekonawo. Cette cérémonie rituelle a été marquée par des invocations adressées aux mânes des ancêtres afin de solliciter leur protection, leur bénédiction et leur bienveillance pour le bon déroulement des festivités. Les officiants ont également formulé des prières en faveur de l’unité, de la paix et du renforcement de la cohésion sociale entre les fils et filles d’Aflao, en particulier ceux de Sagbado. Ils ont aussi imploré la grâce divine sur le Président du Conseil, les membres du gouvernement ainsi que sur l’ensemble des autorités du pays, afin que règnent la paix, la stabilité au Togo. Le représentant du trône de Semekonawo, Togbui Alley-Fiago, a rappelé que Dunenyo Za est une fête de rassemblement qui offre aux fils et filles de la localité un cadre privilégié de retrouvailles entre les générations. Selon lui, cette célébration favorise le raffermissement des liens entre les communautés et contribue à la transmission des valeurs ancestrales aux jeunes. Il a souligné que cette fête constitue également un important levier de promotion du patrimoine culturel local et a encouragé la jeunesse à s’approprier les us et coutumes hérités des ancêtres, afin d’en assurer la préservation et la transmission aux générations futures. L’apothéose est prévue pour le 15 août prochain. ATOP/AO/MD

items.title: L'Iran et Oman avancent sur une nouvelle route maritime dans le détroit d'Ormuz
items.description: L'Iran et Oman ont trouve dans la soiree du 5 août un accord de principe sur le trace d'un nouvel itineraire de transit pour les navires dans le detroit d'Ormuz, selon Teheran. Sa mise en œuvre reste cependant conditionnee a l'evolution des tensions avec les etats-Unis, qui ont impose un blocus des ports iraniens. « Les coordonnees geographiques du trace envisage par les deux parties ont ete approuvees », a declare Esmaïl Baghaï, porte-parole de la diplomatie iranienne. Les deux pays travaillent desormais a une declaration commune, sous reserve qu'« aucune partie tierce ne vienne entrer dans le processus ». Un accord dependant de Washington Le detroit d'Ormuz, par lequel transitait avant la guerre pres d'un cinquieme du commerce mondial des hydrocarbures, est redevenu un point de confrontation majeur depuis la reprise des hostilites entre Washington et Teheran debut juillet. L'Iran affirme vouloir organiser la reouverture avec Oman, autre pays riverain, plutot qu'avec les etats-Unis. Le president americain, Donald Trump, assure pourtant que Teheran souhaite parvenir a un accord avec Washington pour retablir la circulation maritime. Son vice-president, J.D. Vance, a reconnu mercredi 5 août que les negociations etaient difficiles, evoquant des « avancees et des revers » dans les discussions. « ca va etre complique et ca va prendre du temps pour y parvenir », a-t-il declare. Pour Teheran , un eventuel accord avec Mascate ne signifierait pas automatiquement un retour a la libre circulation d'avant-guerre. Esmaïl Baghaï accuse les etats-Unis de maintenir des « actions agressives et menacantes » autour du detroit, notamment via leur blocus naval. La situation reste tendue dans la region : une agence maritime britannique a signale jeudi 6 août qu'un petrolier avait entendu des explosions pres des cotes omanaises, illustrant les risques persistants autour de cette voie maritime strategique.

items.title: 8è édition de Dunenyo Za : Les communautés de Djidjolé sollicitent la bénédiction des ancêtres
items.description: Lomé, 6 août (ATOP) – Le chef du canton de Djidjolé, Togbui Dzidzoli Awounor Détu X, a présidé une cérémonie de libation marquant le lancement des activités de la 8 è édition de Dunenyo Za, le jeudi 6 août à Lomé. Cette édition est placée sous le thème « Avec Dunenyo Za, valorisons la jeunesse et la femme, acteurs du développement durable ». Les organisateurs entendent promouvoir les valeurs culturelles tout en mettant en lumière le rôle de la jeunesse et des femmes dans le développement de la communauté. Séance de danse Le chef du canton de Djidjolé a fait savoir que cette cérémonie de libation a pour objectif d’informer les ancêtres de la tenue de la fête et de solliciter leur protection ainsi que leurs bénédictions pour le bon déroulement des manifestations. « Ce jeudi est un jour sacré consacré aux rituels et à nos divinités. Nous devons informer nos ancêtres de la célébration de cette fête afin qu’ils nous accordent leur grâce et leur bénédiction. C’est dans cet esprit que nous avons organisé cette cérémonie de libation et de sacrifice, afin que Dunenyo Za soit une réussite », a expliqué Togbui Dzidzoli Awounor Détu X. Les activités de cette 8 è édition se poursuivront jusqu’au 15 août, date de l’apothéose. Des jeux traditionnels, des conférences-débats, des journées dédiées à la jeunesse et aux femmes sont prévus. ATOP/MD/AO

items.title: Tivaouane : « Ensemble, penser et agir par le verbe de l’Unicité », thème du Gamou 2026
items.description: Le Comité scientifique du Gamou a publié un document d’orientation destiné à éclairer le thème central de l’édition 1448 H/2026, retenu par le Khalife général des Tidianes, Serigne Babacar Sy Mansour : « Ensemble, penser et agir par le verbe de l’Unicité (Tawhid) ». Ce texte met en avant le Tawhid comme fondement de la foi musulmane, mais aussi comme socle de l’unité, de la cohésion sociale et du vivre-ensemble. Selon le document, la parole de l’Unicité (Lâ ilâha illa Allah) ne se réduit pas à une simple profession de foi. Elle constitue un engagement invitant chaque croyant à faire preuve de sincérité, de justice, de fraternité, de solidarité et de respect d’autrui, en accord avec les enseignements du Saint Coran et de la Sunna. Pour le Comité scientifique, une communauté durablement unie repose sur une croyance authentique, une parole véridique et des comportements exemplaires. Le texte rappelle également que les enseignements de Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy (RTA) s’inscrivent pleinement dans cette vision. Son œuvre a constamment mis l’accent sur la purification des cœurs, l’éducation spirituelle, la quête du savoir et le renforcement des liens fraternels comme conditions de l’épanouissement de la communauté musulmane. Face aux défis sociaux, culturels et numériques, le Comité scientifique appelle les fidèles à faire de la parole un instrument de rapprochement plutôt que de division. Il les invite à privilégier le dialogue, la bienveillance et la responsabilité dans les échanges, y compris sur les espaces numériques, afin de préserver l’unité et la paix sociale. Ce document de référence servira de cadre aux conférences, causeries religieuses et autres activités prévues durant le Gamou 2026. L’ambition est de permettre aux fidèles de s’approprier le message de cette édition et d’en faire un levier de renouveau spirituel, de cohésion communautaire et de promotion du bien commun. Salla GUEYE

items.title: Sandbondtenga: PIVACS lance un tournoi Maracana pour renforcer la résilience des populations de Pissila
items.description: Sandbondtenga: PIVACS lance un tournoi Maracana pour renforcer la résilience des populations de Pissila Pissila, 4 août 2026 (AIB) – L'initiative Pissila vacances culture et sport (PIVACS) a lancé mardi à Pissila la première édition du tournoi Maracana dénommé « La Résilience », sous le thème « Le sport et la culture, facteurs de résilience dans la commune de Pissila ». Cette compétition s’inscrit dans une série d’activités destinées à valoriser la capacité de résilience des populations face aux défis sécuritaires et à rendre hommage aux Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) ainsi qu’aux Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP). « À travers ces activités, nous voulons magnifier et célébrer la paix ainsi que la résilience de nos populations », a indiqué Ben Wahabo Tamou, président de PIVACS, un comité des filles et fils de la commune de Pissila. Selon lui, le tournoi vise également à promouvoir l’union, le patriotisme, la solidarité et le vivre-ensemble dans une commune qui retrouve progressivement sa stabilité grâce aux efforts des FDS, des VDP et à l’engagement des populations. Neuf équipes issues des secteurs et des villages retournés participent à cette compétition qui se déroule jusqu’au 9 août 2026 sur le terrain du marché à volaille de Pissila. Le match d’ouverture a opposé FDS & VDP FC à Saint Jean-Baptiste FC dans un esprit de fair-play. Saint Jean-Baptiste FC à signé sa première victoire sur le score de 2 buts à 0. En plus du Maracana, plusieurs autres activités sont prévues, notamment une course cycliste féminine, un cross populaire suivi d’une séance d’aérobic, un concours de pétanque ainsi que des séances de sensibilisation. La cérémonie de lancement a mobilisé les autorités administratives, militaires et paramilitaires, les leaders coutumiers et religieux, les parrains ainsi que la population. Présidant la cérémonie, Issaka Youma, deuxième vice-président de la délégation spéciale a salué une initiative qui contribue au rapprochement de la jeunesse autour des valeurs de paix, de cohésion sociale et de solidarité. Agence d'information du Burkina KAO/aio/bak

Selon les informations du New York Times, Fulham a transmis une première offre de 23 millions d'euros au Stade Rennais pour s'attacher les services du défenseur central marocain. La proposition du club londonien a toutefois été rejetée par les dirigeants rennais, qui estiment leur joueur à un montant supérieur. Malgré ce refus, Fulham n'aurait pas abandonné le dossier et réfléchirait à revenir avec une offre revue à la hausse, tout en étudiant d'autres pistes pour renforcer sa défense. Âgé de 20 ans et originaire de Marrakech, Aït Boudlal a rejoint le Stade Rennais en 2024. Depuis son arrivée en Bretagne, l'international marocain s'est progressivement imposé, disputant 20 rencontres de Ligue 1 et inscrivant deux buts. S'il n'avait pas été retenu pour disputer la Coupe du monde 2026, le jeune défenseur figurait en revanche dans le groupe du Maroc lors de la dernière Coupe d'Afrique des nations, confirmant son statut de grand espoir des Lions de l'Atlas. Fulham cherche activement à renforcer son secteur défensif après le départ d'Issa Diop vers Ipswich Town. Le club anglais, désormais dirigé par Álvaro Arbeloa, a déjà animé son mercato avec les arrivées de Gonzalo Garcia et Cesar Palacios, recrutés en provenance du Real Madrid. Le dossier Aït Boudlal devrait rester l'un des principaux chantiers des Cottagers d'ici la fermeture du marché des transferts, alors que Rennes entend conserver son jeune défenseur ou obtenir une indemnité à la hauteur de son potentiel. The post Rennes repousse une première offre de Fulham pour Abdelhamid Aït Boudlal appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Daech: l’Afrique au cœur de la menace
items.description: Malgré les revers militaires infligés à son commandement central ces dernières années, le groupe terroriste État islamique en Iraq et au Levant (EIIL), plus connu sous le nom de Daech, continue de représenter une menace sérieuse pour la paix et la sécurité internationales, en particulier en Afrique et en Asie du Sud, ont averti mercredi des hautes responsables des Nations Unies devant le Conseil de sécurité. Présentant le dernier rapport du Secrétaire général sur la menace posée par Daech, Oguljeren Niyazberdiyeva, du Bureau des Nations Unies de lutte contre le terrorisme (UNOCT), a souligné que le groupe terroriste avait profondément transformé son mode de fonctionnement pour survivre aux campagnes militaires menées contre lui. « Malgré les efforts internationaux, Daech continue de poser une grave menace à la paix et à la sécurité internationales », a-t-elle déclaré au nom du chef par intérim de l’UNOCT, Alexandre Zouev. UN Photo/Eskinder Debebe Oguljeren Niyazberdiyeva, du Bureau des Nations Unies de lutte contre le terrorisme, s'adresse au Conseil de sécurité réuni sur les menaces à la paix et à la sécurité internationales causées par des actes terroristes. Un groupe plus dispersé mais toujours dangereux Selon le rapport, les opérations antiterroristes ont considérablement affaibli la direction centrale de Daech et réduit sa capacité à planifier et coordonner des attaques complexes à l'échelle internationale. Toutefois, cette pression n'a pas fait disparaître la menace. Le groupe s'est progressivement transformé en un réseau décentralisé de filiales régionales, liées par une idéologie commune et bénéficiant d'une plus grande autonomie opérationnelle. Cette évolution lui permet de s'adapter plus facilement aux contextes locaux et de poursuivre ses activités malgré les pertes subies. L'ONU estime ainsi que le risque terroriste demeure particulièrement élevé dans plusieurs régions d'Afrique, où certaines branches de Daech continuent d'étendre leur influence. L'Afrique au cœur des préoccupations Le rapport identifie le Sahel et le bassin du lac Tchad comme les principaux foyers d'expansion du groupe. La Province de l'État islamique en Afrique de l'Ouest (ISWAP) reste aujourd'hui la filiale la plus active de Daech dans le monde. Selon les Nations Unies, elle poursuit son développement militaire tout en recourant de plus en plus à des drones commerciaux afin d'améliorer ses capacités de surveillance et d'attaque. En République démocratique du Congo (RDC) et au Mozambique, les groupes affiliés poursuivent également leurs offensives malgré la pression exercée par les forces nationales et régionales. Ils continuent parallèlement à recruter de nouveaux combattants et à renforcer leurs réseaux locaux. Pour les Nations Unies, cette dynamique illustre la capacité de Daech à exploiter les fragilités institutionnelles, les conflits prolongés et les difficultés économiques pour étendre son implantation. Des inquiétudes persistantes en Syrie et en Afghanistan En Syrie, l'évolution du contexte politique et sécuritaire modifie également la nature de la menace. L'ONU s'inquiète notamment des conséquences de la fermeture, en février dernier, du camp d'Al-Hol. Les autorités ne savent plus où se trouvent plusieurs milliers d'anciens résidents, ce qui fait craindre une dispersion de personnes potentiellement liées à Daech. Les Nations Unies réitèrent leur appel au rapatriement « sûr, volontaire et digne » des personnes concernées, conformément au droit international. En Iraq, les autorités ont réussi à réduire de manière significative les capacités opérationnelles du groupe. Mais Mme Niyazberdiyeva a insisté sur la nécessité de consolider ces progrès. Selon elle, la lutte contre le terrorisme ne peut se limiter aux seules opérations militaires. Elle passe également par le renforcement des institutions publiques, une justice efficace, ainsi que des programmes de réhabilitation et de réinsertion destinés aux anciens combattants et à leurs familles. En Asie du Sud, la branche État islamique au Khorasan (EI-K) demeure l'une des plus préoccupantes. Le rapport estime qu'elle conserve la capacité d'inspirer ou de soutenir des attentats au-delà des frontières afghanes, tout en profitant de l'instabilité régionale pour recruter de nouveaux membres et préparer d'autres opérations. Les nouvelles technologies au service du terrorisme L'ONU alerte également sur l'utilisation croissante des nouvelles technologies par Daech. Selon le rapport, le groupe terroriste exploite désormais l'intelligence artificielle, les plateformes numériques, les communications chiffrées, les actifs virtuels et les drones sans pilote afin d'adapter ses méthodes de propagande, de recrutement, de financement et de planification. Pour l'ONU, cette évolution rend indispensable un renforcement de la coopération internationale, mais aussi un dialogue plus étroit avec les entreprises technologiques et le secteur privé afin d'améliorer la gouvernance de ces outils émergents. Toutefois ces mêmes technologies peuvent également devenir de puissants instruments de prévention et de lutte contre le terrorisme lorsqu'elles sont utilisées de manière responsable et dans le respect du droit international. UN Photo/ Manuel Elías Carmen G. Cantor, directrice exécutive adjointe de la Direction exécutive du Comité contre le terrorisme (CTED), lors d'une réunion du Conseil de sécurité sur les menaces à la paix et à la sécurité internationales causées par des actes terroristes. Un « écosystème » terroriste en ligne Intervenant également devant le Conseil de sécurité, la Directrice exécutive adjointe de la Direction exécutive du Comité contre le terrorisme, Carmen G. Cantor, a mis en garde contre l'essor d'un véritable « écosystème » numérique qui favorise la radicalisation. Selon elle, les groupes terroristes exploitent désormais les réseaux sociaux, les plateformes de jeux en ligne et les services de messagerie chiffrée pour diffuser leur propagande, recruter de nouveaux membres et lever des fonds. Face à une menace toujours plus diffuse, technologique et transnationale, Mme Niyazberdiyeva et Mme Cantor ont appelé les États à maintenir leur coopération et à privilégier des réponses globales qui associent sécurité, prévention, développement et respect des droits humains. Source: ONU Info L’article Daech: l'Afrique au cœur de la menace est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Koulsé/Développement: le PARD 2026 affiche un taux d’exécution physique de 22,90 % à mi-parcours
items.description: Koulsé/Développement: le PARD 2026 affiche un taux d'exécution physique de 22,90 % à mi-parcours Kaya, 31 juil. 2026 (AIB) – Le Cadre régional de développement (CRD) de la région des Koulsé a tenu, vendredi à Kaya, sa deuxième session ordinaire de l'année consacrée à la revue à mi-parcours du Plan d'action régional de développement (PARD), faisant état d'un taux d'exécution physique de 22,90 % et d'un taux d'exécution financière de 23,09 % au 30 juin 2026. La secrétaire général de la région des Koulsé, Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé représentant le gouverneur a indiqué que cette revue visait à examiner et valider le rapport régional de performance à mi-parcours 2026 relatif à la mise en œuvre du PARD, à dresser le bilan du premier semestre, à analyser les difficultés rencontrées et à proposer des mesures correctives. Selon les résultats présentés, 31 produits sur les 135 programmés ont été réalisés, soit un taux d'exécution physique de 22,90 %. Sur le plan financier, 6,281 milliards de FCFA ont été engagés sur une prévision de 27,2 milliards de FCFA, représentant un taux d'exécution de 23,09 %. Le PARD actualisé fait ressortir un besoin de financement de 49,903 milliards de FCFA, soit 91,21 % du coût global prévu pour la période 2026-2027. La secrétaire générale a relevé que ces performances, bien qu'en deçà des attentes, traduisent les efforts consentis par les acteurs dans un contexte marqué par les défis sécuritaires, la réduction des appuis des partenaires et les contraintes budgétaires. Saluant l'engagement des services techniques, des collectivités territoriales et des partenaires, camarade Adenyo/Sermé les a exhortés à poursuivre leurs efforts avec détermination, dans un esprit d'anticipation et d'innovation, afin d'accélérer l'exécution des actions programmées et d'améliorer la qualité des services publics offerts aux populations. Agence d'Information du Burkina AIO/bak

items.title: Conseils médicaux pour bien traverser la vague de chaleur
items.description: Les températures grimpent, et avec elles, le risque pour la santé. Comment bien traverser ces journées caniculaires ? Mauvais sommeil, maux de tête et problèmes de concentration : la chaleur pèse sur le corps et l'esprit. Dans le pire des cas, elle peut devenir mortelle. Avec le changement climatique, les vagues de chaleur deviennent plus fréquentes, plus intenses et plus longues – devenant ainsi l’un des plus grands risques pour la santé en été. Comment se protéger, quels signaux d'alarme prendre au sérieux et quels mythes sur la chaleur ont la vie dure ? En ma qualité de médecin pédiatre, voici ce que je conseille. Dr Salem Sahli * La chaleur représente un stress pour l’organisme. Lors de températures élevées, le cœur, les reins et la circulation sanguine tournent à plein régime. L’organisme tente de maintenir sa température corporelle constante. Et cela coûte de l’énergie avec pour conséquences des problèmes circulatoires, des maux de tête et des difficultés de concentration. Les personnes particulièrement vulnérables sont les personnes âgées, les jeunes enfants et les personnes souffrant de maladies cardiovasculaires ou d’autres maladies chroniques. Mais la chaleur peut s’avérer très dangereuse même pour les personnes en bonne santé. Même si l'on se sent en forme, il convient d’adapter son quotidien lors des journées de canicule et de renoncer durant la journée à tout ce qui fatigue le corps, qu’il s'agisse du jardinage ou du sport. L’une des règles les plus importantes est de boire suffisamment. En transpirant, le corps ne perd pas seulement de l’eau, mais aussi des minéraux. C’est pourquoi toute personne qui transpire abondamment doit non seulement boire en quantité suffisante, mais aussi veiller à un apport adéquat en électrolytes, par exemple via des boissons isotoniques. Le corps souffre d’une vague de chaleur de jour comme de nuit. Si les températures ne descendent pas en dessous de 20°C, on parle de nuit tropicale. L’organisme peut alors à peine se régénérer, car il doit continuer à dépenser de l’énergie pendant le sommeil pour se refroidir. Ceux qui ont du mal à s’endormir devraient appliquer des compresses fraîches, prendre une douche tiède avant de se coucher et n’utiliser qu’une couverture légère. Je déconseille en revanche les douches glacées qui ont tendance à stimuler le corps plutôt qu’à le détendre. Un rafraîchissement doux, comme un bain de pieds froid, est bien plus judicieux. Les personnes sous traitement médical doivent redoubler de vigilance les jours de forte chaleur. La perte d’eau réduit le volume sanguin, ce qui augmente la concentration de certains médicaments dans le sang. Les médicaments agissent alors différemment. Cela concerne surtout les antihypertenseurs et les diurétiques. La chaleur pouvant abaisser davantage la pression artérielle, le dosage doit être adapté avec le médecin traitant, jamais de son propre chef. Lors de la prise d’antalgiques, il faut veiller à boire beaucoup pour maintenir une bonne irrigation des reins. Les sédatifs, quant à eux, peuvent atténuer les signaux d’alarme émis par le corps. Il est également essentiel de conserver les médicaments au frais et au sec, conformément à la notice. Les jours de canicule, il faut être attentif aux signaux d’alerte : si l’on ne se sent pas bien, qu’on a des vertiges, des maux de tête ou des démarches hésitantes, il faut prendre cela au sérieux. La règle est alors de se mettre immédiatement à l’ombre ou dans un endroit frais, de s’asseoir ou de s’allonger, et de refroidir progressivement son corps. Si des symptômes tels que des crampes musculaires, des difficultés respiratoires ou des malaises circulatoires apparaissent, il faut contacter immédiatement les secours. La chaleur n’affecte pas seulement le corps – elle impacte aussi le mental. Les gens sont plus irritables, plus agressifs et souffrent plus souvent d’anxiété. Une étude américaine menée sur 45 ans a montré que les violences augmentent les jours de canicule. En plus du potentiel d’agressivité, le risque de suicide augmente également. Le corps est tellement concentré sur la régulation de sa température que le moindre stress supplémentaire le surcharge rapidement. De plus, l’équilibre hormonal est perturbé. Le cerveau sécrète davantage d’hormones de stress comme le cortisol ou l’adrénaline, ce qui peut favoriser l’agitation, l’anxiété et les états dépressifs. Insolation, coup de chaleur ou malaises : lors des journées chaudes, les services d’urgence sont sollicités bien plus souvent qu’à l’accoutumée. Bien souvent, un simple coup d’œil et un contact tactile suffisent pour identifier le problème. La chaleur monte dans le corps, les gens ont souvent le visage très rouge. Quand on touche leur peau, elle est totalement sèche parce qu’ils ont déjà évacué toute leur transpiration. Les personnes âgées sont particulièrement exposées. Elles ne boivent pas assez et sont souvent habillées trop chaudement. Je suis souvent surpris, en me promenant en ville, de voir que même par forte chaleur, les personnes âgées restent habillées de façon très stricte. Au lieu de pantalons longs et de chemises, des tissus clairs et légers sont recommandés. Les courses ou les promenades doivent être planifiées de préférence tôt le matin ou en soirée. Pour éviter que les logements ne surchauffent, il faut aérer à fond tôt le matin, puis garder fenêtres et volets fermés. On n’aère à nouveau que lorsque la température extérieure baisse en soirée. Il est également conseillé de privilégier des repas légers, une consommation d’eau suffisante et un peu moins de café afin d’éviter de surcharger le système cardiovasculaire. * Médecin pédiatre. items.title: Pénuries de médicaments, médecins non payés... le système de santé palestinien au bord de l'effondrement
items.description: Les centres de santé publics palestiniens fonctionnent seulement une ou deux fois par semaine, les hôpitaux sont submergés et n’assurent que les urgences, les médecins sont partiellement payés et il y a des pénuries de médicaments. Le rapport de l’ONG Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) pointe la responsabilité des autorités israéliennes qui refusent de verser les taxes douanières prélevées au nom de l’Autorité palestinienne. Le blocage de ces recettes fiscales met en péril l'accès aux soins en Cisjordanie occupée. Pour de nombreux Palestiniens, les cliniques mobiles de Physicians for Human Rights Israel figurent désormais parmi les seules structures à combler ce vide.

items.title: Fed Up With Romance
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Reports confirming the death of young love are pouring in: Post-COVID declines in dating aren’t rebounding. Way fewer teens and young adults are having sex. In 2019, 42 percent of single adults younger than 40 told Pew Research Center that they’d never been in a committed relationship. Thirty years ago, my friends and I thought of romance and marriage much the same way screenwriters did: They were just the expected ending. Now this attitude seems to be less and less the norm. It’s not that people don’t want romantic relationships. But chasing them feels to people like it exacts too much of a toll. So over time, they’ve become less of a priority. As a result, we have entered what The Atlantic ’s staff writer Faith Hill calls the “ great romance slump ,” in which romance is no longer the center of people’s lives. Hill created a survey and sent it to people all over the country. She heard from men, women, nonbinary people, queer people, and straight people. From their answers and insights from research, Hill came up with solid theories about why more people are giving up on love. On this week’s Radio Atlantic, Hill explains what’s driving the romance slump, and what its long-term implications are for families, the economy, and politics. And we hear from two people Hill interviewed who have given up, at least for now. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: It didn’t happen all at once. Instead, the modern disenchantment with romance unfolded slowly, subtly, but still unmistakably. Post COVID, young people stopped dating as much. If you talk to them about why, what you hear is exhaustion with the apps—the whole hassle of combing through matches, chatting, finding a mutually convenient time, and then dragging yourself out of the house to meet a total stranger. All of that started to seem less important than seeing friends, caring for family, getting some work done, watching the series that everyone else was talking about. These shifts were made one by one, inside people’s heads. And then all of these individual decisions accumulated over time and turned into something new, something which staff writer Faith Hill calls the romance slump. Rosin: I have a question for you, as my colleague. Are you the romance reporter? Is that your actual job? Faith Hill: ( Laughs .) You know, I’m proud to hold that mantle. I report on some other things, too, but romance and dating and singlehood specifically has kind of become a big thing for me. Rosin: That’s amazing. So The Atlantic has a romance-and-relationship reporter, and that is you. Hill: I guess so. [ Music ] Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . Faith spent the last several months reporting on what she called the great romance slump. In the last 40 or so years, we’ve seen huge drops in both marriage and cohabitation rates, especially among 25-to-34-year-olds. Hill: But there’s also just a shrinking share of young adults who have a steady partner. And, you know, in 2019, 42 percent of single adults younger than 40 told Pew Research Center that they’d never been in a committed relationship. Rosin: That is the statistic that really surprised me. Hill: I felt the same when I saw that, and I think it’s important to talk about because it’s pretty easy to shrug off the declining marriage rates as kind of: The institution of marriage is not as important to people. You can easily have romance without marriage. Rosin: Or intimacy without marriage, or children without marriage. Hill: Right. Exactly. But that’s not the only thing going on. You know, it’s not just about sort of views towards marriage, and I think this is really quite a profound change. Rosin: Listening to you, I see why you called your story “The Great Romance Slump,” because it is something of a resignation. It’s kind of like a shrug. Faith: Yes. That’s exactly it. I liked the term for that reason. It, you know, has this kind of subtle, almost passive feel to it. You know, it’s not a sudden and dramatic plummet. It’s not that active. Like, it’s not people all swearing off romance, but rather sort of a lot of people kind of slowly giving up on it kind of captures this pessimism and fatigue. Rosin: Yeah. It’s like a slight bad smell in the air. Faith: Yeah, exactly. But it also implies that it’s not necessarily permanent. You know, you can come back from a slump, so there’s that too. Rosin: Okay, let’s get into some of the reasons this is happening. Some I can just guess right off the bat. I did write a book called The End of Men about a decade ago, so I did a lot of study into how men’s and women’s relationships were changing, and just the basic fact of women being more financially independent, women being able to buy houses. We can have credit cards now—amazing—have any career you want. So the basic idea that you need a man in order to survive is just not true anymore. What are some of the other reasons that you came across? Or at least, what’s your take on the cause? Hill: I think that there’s kind of a combination of people needing romance less than they used to, which is great, and also dating being hard in these, you know, very specific frustrating ways. You hear so much about the dating apps, of when people talk about singlehood and romance, and a lot of times, I think people are talking about the sort of distance of the technology making it easier to ghost and people being on bad behavior because of that, kind of a lack of accountability. [ Music ] Hill: And also, you hear a lot about the kind of paradox of choice—like, people are just swimming in options. And I think there’s truth there. But I do kind of think, you know, the big thing that comes to mind for me when I consider online dating is just the toll that it takes on people. You know, when you’re having to set aside time and energy and money to meet strangers, to suss them out on the app, and then meet up with them, and then, you know, try to keep the momentum up, it just is a huge toll. And, you know, I think that toll means that a lot of people, like, want a relationship but aren’t going to prioritize it. But I think the combination of dating being kind of exhausting and time-consuming and requiring sacrifice from other areas of life, and singlehood being so normal and doable, it starts to make it very easy for romance to just, like, not be the top thing that you wanna pursue. And, you know, when you want romance but don’t need it, and you don’t feel like it’s gonna be easy to get, and you don’t feel optimistic about those chances or about the people you would be dating, a lot of people are just gonna give it up. Rosin: And so if you were a sociologist, what would be the sentence? Like, what is the headline in the world of romance that merits bigger attention? Hill: Well, I would say, you know, romance is obviously a very broad term. Under that umbrella, you know, you might fit sex, dating, partnership, marriage. But all of these forms, particularly among young people, seem to be on the decline. And I think that shift has a lot of downstream implications. You know, it’s changing how and whether people have families, how people spend their time, how they spend their money, potentially who they vote for. And, you know, if romance is no longer the center of nearly everyone’s life, something else is. [ Music ] Rosin: How fed up with romance do people have to be before they give up? The line is different for everyone, but there are some patterns in people’s breaking points. Faith created a survey and sent it far and wide—she heard back from men, women, nonbinary people, queer, straight, and living in all different parts of the country. One loud theme that emerges, from the respondents but also from the research, is a gender gap—more women giving up on men, not trusting them to be supportive in the right ways, not getting what they need from them, and not willing to give so much when they’re not getting back. One of the people that Faith talked to was a woman named Treasure, who drifted away from romance and then did find new things to put at the center of her life. Hill: Treasure is a 39-year-old woman in Chicago who has been single for a long time, and she’s loving it. Treasure: I have been single now for 10 years. Hill: She, for many years, was trying to date seriously, trying to find someone to marry. She was, you know, really a romantic and had high hopes about it. Treasure: From 18 to about 27, I took dating very seriously. Hill: She was engaged four different times. In each one, she felt like she was contributing half financially, and yet she was also doing all of the child care. She has three children. Treasure: I already had two children before I turned 18. I started off as a teen mother. All four relationships failed because it’s like raising another child. Hill: After that fourth relationship ended, the fourth engagement, that was really the last straw for her. Treasure: I’m going to get extremely personal here, but I had a miscarriage, and my significant other at the time noticed that I was depressed and noticed that I was upset, and I kept trying to explain to him, “Well, you know, my hormones are changing right now.” I was already four months along. I was like, “I’m really sad right now. I know you feel like you need attention, but right now I can’t do this. This isn’t about you.” Hill: She said, “You know, the one time that I need something from him, his support, he couldn’t be there.” Treasure: In my mind, it was like I overperform in these relationships, and when it comes down to the wire and something is needed for me from them, I was not receiving it. And if that’s the case, then what is the purpose? Hill: I think she just felt really exhausted by holding everyone else up and feeling like the mother to the partners she had. Treasure: That was the last time for me. I was like, “This isn’t for me.” [ Music ] Hill: She likes to say, you know, she realized if she wasn’t gonna find a husband, she had to make “husband money.” So she did a bunch of training and an apprenticeship, and she ended up becoming a technical engineer in a union job, and that totally changed the financial picture for her, where she felt like, you know, she could be single and take care of her kids herself. Treasure: I've been in the trades now for nine years, and I choose not to date anymore. Hill: When she first gave up on dating and romance, she felt really lonely. I think it was a big change. But she realized she just had to start replacing what she had gotten from those partnerships with other things. Treasure: I adjusted, and I made more friends, and I found myself again. I have new hobbies and go places alone. I travel alone. I go to the movies alone. I go out to dinner alone. I’m literally dating myself, and I’m so much happier. I am the one for me. Hill: She wishes that she could have found the relationship that she once dreamed about, but she said, “I think at this point, it’s a fantasy.” Treasure: It’s kinda like, How do you get it all? Is there a way? I haven’t found it. I had to give up romantic love with a spouse in order to achieve everything else that I wanted. Rosin: That’s so interesting. It’s like when Esther Perel says we look to our partners and we expect everything from them, and that’s not realistic. It sounds like she just took the everything and divided it among people—like, I’m gonna have best friends here. I’m gonna have a community there. I’m gonna make money here , and maybe she just has sex somewhere else. You know? Hill: Right. Exactly. Rosin: I bet that there are women who can definitely relate to that. Does she seem happy to you now? Hill: She really does seem happy. Yeah. She was, I think, one of the happiest people I talked to for this story. I found that really beautiful to kind of realize that if you can sort of round that bend psychologically, sometimes you just can grow to love your life in the way it is if you sort of lean into it. I don’t think it would necessarily be the same for everyone, but Treasure is really independent, and she has great friendships and meaningful work. I think she just had such a hard time trying to find love that, in comparison, she feels so free. Rosin: It’s important, because I guess she counts as a post-romance model. Like, it’s not for everyone, but that is a template that might work for some people. Because she did wanna have a romantic relationship at some point. She sought it. She tried many times. And so for anyone in that situation, this is an alternate model that’s maybe hopeful at the other side. Did you have a sense of how typical she was? Hill: Yeah, I’ve talked to a lot of people who have sort of stopped searching for romance. I think she might be a little atypical in just how much she’s loving it and thriving. But I’ve talked to a lot of people who say that they would welcome a relationship if it fell in their lap, but they’re not gonna search for it. They just can’t do that anymore. They’re too exhausted. They spent too much time on it. They wanna focus on other things. And I actually talked to one researcher who said, you know, she had to stop asking in studies whether people were “actively” looking for a relationship, because what resonated more with people was whether they were “open” to a relationship. [ Music ] Rosin: It’s also interesting because the word slump is sort of a negative word, but Treasure’s case implies that the romance slump is not necessarily a negative thing, because it does open up alternate possibilities, particularly for women. Hill: I think that’s definitely the hope. And, you know, I think for some people like Treasure, who can kind of pull this off and find meaning and community in all these other ways, it could be really beautiful. And of course, it is a great thing that this change is happening, partly because women are able to live independently and focus on other things. So I definitely don’t think the shift is all negative. At the same time, you know, the majority of single people do still say that they want a long-term partnership. And so for me, that’s kind of at the heart of this story. You know, what happens to the people who want love and are struggling to find it or give up on it altogether? I do think that there’s real loss there that we can take seriously, even if, you know, it does open up sort of new ways to think about purpose and community and meaning. Rosin: Next up: the men. What’s their experience of the romance slump? That’s after the break. [ Break ] Rosin: Okay. We’ve talked about the women’s point of view. What about the men? I wanna talk about one of the guys you interviewed, Arthur. Can you tell me about him? Hill: Arthur is a guy in his 40s who has spent many years dating. He’s had one-off dates here and there. He’s dated some people for a month or so. He’s had some one-to-two-year relationships. But he’s always felt like it just kind of hasn’t totally worked out. Arthur: It was always kinda like hedged by them saying stuff like, “Oh, you’re nice and everything. We’ve had some good times, but honestly, you’re not really right for me.” Hill: Some exes have kind of told him that they feel like he’s almost too nice. Arthur: I’m not sure how to square that. Like, I mean, I will be, you know, the man and, you know, make all the plans and execute and everything if you want. Hill: You know, they want him to kind of be more decisive or be the man in the relationship. Arthur: But I mean, that does kinda come at the cost of me being somewhat less, you know, supportive and more demanding, because it kinda has to be that way. Hill: One person said that he has “dad” energy. Arthur: I’m not 100 percent sure what that means, but I’m guessing it’s not very sexy. Rosin: Ugh. Hill: Right? Rosin: That’s trauma. I mean, that could be great, I guess, but it sounds like he did not take it as a good thing. Hill: Right, and I think this person didn’t take it as a good thing in the romantic context. She wasn’t looking for “dad” energy. Rosin: Yeah. That gets into something very important, which is the impossible dilemma that men seem to be in. It’s very hard to know how to be, because you mentioned earlier that part of the problem between Treasure, who we talked about, and lots of women, was that men could not see their needs or weren’t open or communicative enough. And yet, here is poor Arthur maybe trying to be that way and getting dinged for it. Did you hear men talk about their confusion over roles? Hill: Yeah, absolutely. I think we’re in a kind of confusing in-between time, where there are sort of these new standards for men that they’re trying to reach, like this—you know, being kind and communicative and emotionally open—but at the same time, the old standards haven’t really gone away fully. So a lot of men did still feel like they were expected to pay for everything on the dates and, kind of, take the lead on everything, initiate flirting, kissing. And they felt sort of torn between those two and confused. Like, they were trying to kind of exemplify all of these traits at once—like, be sort of masculine and sturdy, but also gentle and empathetic—and feeling like they were sort of always falling down on the job on one of those sides. Rosin: And did Arthur have any positive experiences? Like, did he have any success or things that worked for him? Hill: He definitely had some, you know, relationships that ended in friendships. And so it hasn’t been all, you know, a bad time. And yet, I think he felt like he was just putting so much into it. You know, he still very deeply wants to find love. Arthur: I’m human, right? Like, I want to go out and, like, meet people and, you know, kiss the pretty ladies and all that. Hill: But he just feels like he can’t be prioritizing it anymore. Arthur: There’s so much going on. I’ve got all this stuff that I need to learn. I wanna go play with my niece and my nephew. You know what I mean? So something had to give, and I decided it was kinda like, You know what? This romantic stuff is not going my way anyway. Instead of being, like, top three things in my life, let’s bring it down to, like, maybe the bottom of the top 10 . Hill: He’s kind of pulled back from it. He’s focusing on being a good uncle, a good person, a good employee. So he’s like, “Let me just focus on myself and being the best person I can be,” and that has been a real sort of grief that he’s carrying. Arthur: It really broke my heart to feel like I wouldn’t find my person. Like, it really did. I carried that. It was like I lost a parent. Like, it really felt that hard. Hill: He feels like he kind of had to at least temporarily say goodbye to this partner he kept expecting to show up. Rosin: Did Arthur have a moment in the same way that Treasure did? Like, a moment where he thought—you know, like Treasure’s miscarriage moment—where he thought, I gotta stop ? Hill: I think for him, it was a little bit more gradual over time, like, just realizing sort of how draining this was. He also talked about COVID. There was a huge pandemic dating recession, and a big part of that was just young people not meeting as much. You know, the singlehood rates rose a lot after COVID. But there’s also another element, which is something that Arthur talked about, which is, you know, feeling like he actually lost some social skills when he was isolating in COVID. You know, he just was, obviously, not seeing people as much for a long time, and then when the world kind of opened up there, you know, it takes a while to sort of get back into the social life you used to have. Arthur: The world fully started opening up again, and I found myself feeling awkward. You know, it’s like being 17 again and, like, afraid to talk to the pretty girl you see. Hill: I think a lot of people can relate to that, right? Like, in the dating context or otherwise, just, like, feeling weirdly socially rusty. And that does not make making good chat and being charming with a stranger easy. Like, dating is already pretty hard socially. Rosin: Yeah. Yeah. You said that Arthur was focusing on other things. How do you hear something like that? Like, do you hear that to mean he’s given up on romance? He’s not actively dating? Hill: I think that’s kind of one of the big questions of this piece, you know: How much is this a sad thing for people, or how much is it kind of a triumph that people can have other priorities? And I think it’s a big mix. You know, I do think he has a meaningful and full life, and he’s getting a lot of purpose and enrichment from the relationships and the hobbies he does have. But at the same time, you know, he says himself that he is yearning for a partner. You know, he wants to do all of this with someone. Arthur: I do wanna find somebody that I can wake up in the morning and snuggle with, you know, for the next 20 or 30 years. Hill: And so I think it’s kind of both at once. You know, I’m very happy for him that he is able to find meaning in these other ways and that he has taken kind of, you know, a break from dating when it was not feeling good. But at the same time, he’s not getting something that he wants. And I want that for him. Rosin: So you’re a romance reporter. You’re also an adult woman looking for a long-term partnership. So I’m curious what this reporting experience has done to your outlook. Did you talk to all these people and feel comforted and more hopeful? Or did you talk to all these people and think, Oh, we just have to really accept a new reality ? Like, We are entering a kind of post-romance, post-marriage age, and we have to be creative about how we adapt to it ? Hill: Yeah, it’s a little bit of both. I definitely feel comfort in the sense that there are so many great people who just have been struggling with this for a really long time, and it does make one feel less alone in it. So there’s something really important about knowing there are, like, structural forces at work and a lot of luck too. Rosin: Like, It’s not just me . Like, The world is conspiring against me in some way . Hill: Right. Exactly. But at the same time, of course, that makes you feel, like, a little more pessimistic, right? Because it’s not like I can just change something about myself. It’s like, yeah, you know, dating is really hard right now, and a lot of people are in this situation. And we can’t just sort of fix all of the things that are making it hard. Rosin: Yeah. You’ve mentioned the yearning a couple of times. I wonder if that made you pessimistic or hopeful. Like, when I think of tens of thousands of young people yearning for a partner, it makes me sad, but maybe also makes me happy. Like, it’s a motivating factor. How did you receive that? Hill: Yeah, I think the yearning is kind of a beautiful thing. I mean, it’s a human emotion, you know? It can be positive in that it drives people forward to look for something that they really want. And I love to hear when people can sort of find peace with singlehood and close that door if that makes their life better. And yet, at the same time, I think that’s the thing with the slump, right? Like, a lot of people who do want partnership are just kind of giving up. And I think the yearning is one thing that is gonna kind of keep people having hope and still trying. You know, I wouldn’t want all of that to go away. And I also hope that, you know, people can maybe channel the yearning into other parts of life. Like, I do think there’s not such a clear objective divide between the romantic and other forms of love and passion. And, you know, I think maybe these single people who are turning their attention elsewhere are really bringing a lot of their heart and soul because they’re looking for other ways to kind of fill the center of their life and, like, give love. And I think that makes them—it gives them sort of a powerful energy. Rosin: Yeah. Can I ask: Did you shift in any way? Like, after doing all of this reporting and talking to all of these people and finding all of this company in the looking for romance in an ambivalent way, did you make any decisions about your own life? Hill: I didn’t make any clear ones, but I will say, you know, when I talk to people who have stopped dating—and, you know, a lot of those people are enjoying their life more now than when they were dating, ’cause they weren’t having a good time; that’s why they stopped. So it does, it feels pretty tempting, and I do start to think, you know, of all the different things I could be doing with my time. Like, I feel like I might be a better daughter and a better friend, and maybe I could, like, start writing fiction or—you know, my mind starts racing, and I think those are good things to be thinking about. We all do have limited time on this Earth, and we have to make choices about how to use it. So that’s something I’m considering, but I also know that some people I talk to, you know, when I checked in after we had an interview, they had had, you know, some dates with someone they were really excited about. I talked to at least one person who was like, “Oh, I found someone. Like, he’s the one. I am not right for your story anymore.” So that also was a reminder that, you know, if you do keep trying, for a lot of people, eventually, like, there is, you know, someone who makes the rest of it all feel like it was worth it to lead to that. So I’m split. [ Music ] Rosin: Ugh. We can never give up on the rom-com ending. Hill: Yeah. Rosin: It’s just how we are. We’re just built that way. Well, Faith, thank you so much for joining me today. Hill: Thank you so much. Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes with help from Jacob Smollen and Jinae West. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Fact-checking by Genevieve Finn and Álex Maroño Porto. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: Zoundwéogo/Excellence scolaire: Une association récompense les meilleurs élèves et enseignants de la CEB de Bindé
items.description: Zoundwéogo/Excellence scolaire: Une association récompense les meilleurs élèves et enseignants de la CEB de Bindé Bindé, 1er août 2026 (AIB) – L’Association des Jeunes Unis pour le Développement du Zoundwéogo (AJUDPZ) a récompensé, samedi à Bindé, les meilleurs élèves, enseignants et acteurs de l’éducation de la Circonscription d’éducation de base (CEB), en reconnaissance de leurs performances aux examens du Certificat d’études primaires (CEP) et du concours d’entrée en classe de sixième, marqués par un taux de réussite de 97 %. Cette initiative de l’AJUDPZ vise à promouvoir la culture de l’excellence et à encourager les élèves ainsi que les enseignants à poursuivre leurs efforts en vue d’améliorer les résultats scolaires. Le premier de la CEB, Compaoré Landry, élève de l’école primaire publique de Ouda, a reçu un vélo en récompense de ses excellentes performances. Il s’agit du troisième vélo qu’il obtient grâce à ses résultats scolaires. La première de la CEB, Nikiema Rosalie Ivonne, de l’école primaire publique de Koankin, a également été récompensée par un vélo, le deuxième qu’elle reçoit en raison de ses brillants résultats. Les autres élèves méritants ont reçu des kits scolaires destinés à les accompagner dans la poursuite de leur cursus. Au cours de la cérémonie, plusieurs enseignants ainsi que des personnalités ayant contribué au rayonnement de l’éducation dans la commune ont été honorés par des attestations de reconnaissance et des lettres de félicitations. La CEB de Bindé a également bénéficié d’un ordinateur portable offert par l’AJUDPZ afin de renforcer ses capacités de gestion administrative. Le Chef de la Circonscription d’éducation de base (CCEB) de Bindé, Issouf Kabré, a salué cette initiative, qu’il a qualifiée de contribution majeure à la promotion de l’excellence scolaire. Il a exprimé sa gratitude aux responsables de l’AJUDPZ pour leur engagement constant en faveur de l’éducation. Le chef de canton de Bindé, Naaba Yanbolobo II, a, lui aussi, félicité l’association pour son accompagnement des acteurs de l’éducation et a invité les élèves à persévérer dans l’effort et la discipline. La cérémonie s’est achevée par la remise de distinctions à plusieurs personnalités reconnues pour leur soutien au développement de l’éducation dans la commune de Bindé. Elle a réuni les autorités administratives, coutumières et religieuses de la commune, ainsi que de nombreux acteurs du système éducatif. Agence d’information du Burkina HO/BGB/bak

items.title: PM Shehbaz departs for Saudi Arabia on 3-day visit
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday left for a three-day visit to Saudi Arabia, where he will be accompanied by the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. In a post on X, the government said that the premier has left for the visit at the invitation of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Apart from CDF Munir, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, and Special Assistant Tariq Fatemi will also accompany the premier on the visit. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar, who is currently in Saudi Arabia after concluding a visit to Jordan, will be part of the delegation as well. The premier will also perform Umrah and visit Holy Prophet’s (PBUH) mosque in Madina during the visit, the government said. Earlier, FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi announced the visit in a weekly briefing. “During the visit, the prime minister will meet the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and discussions will focus on consolidating the Pakistan-Saudi bilateral relationship and exchange views on areas of regional and international developments of mutual interests,” he said. He stressed that the visit marked Pakistan’s “long-standing partnership” with Saudi Arabia, which he said was “anchored in decades of mutual trust, cooperation and brotherhood”. Andrabi noted that while the visit was taking place amid heightened tensions in the Gulf, he said that “it will carry immense significance beyond the immediate crisis and short-term considerations”. He added that the visit will “further strengthen bilateral relations, deepen strategic cooperation, enhance coordination on regional and international issues of mutual interest and also reinforce multilateral cooperation”. Shortly after, an official statement regarding the visit was also issued. The premier had last visited Saudi Arabia in April, meeting with the kingdom’s top leadership. As the Middle East conflict has expanded across new fronts, Saudi Arabia has unveiled plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition to protect shipping and energy supply routes in the Red Sea region. Fourteen countries, including Pakistan, have voiced support for the coalition. In July, Pakistan also endorsed Saudi Arabia’s air strikes in Iraq as an exercise of its right to self-defence. The remarks came two days after Saudi Arabia and the US carried out coordinated strikes against installations of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Units, accusing elements within the umbrella force of launching attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The remarks followed Pakistan’s earlier warning after Yemen’s Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade targeting shipping linked to Saudi Arabia. Islamabad had then described attacks on Pakistani maritime interests as a “red line”, warning that any hostile action against Pakistani-flagged vessels or commercial shipping would be treated as an attack on Pakistan. The country also simultaneously reaffirmed its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security and the uninterrupted flow of lawful maritime commerce through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb. Last year, Islamabad and Riyadh concluded a Strategic Mutual Defence Agree­ment, which became operational earlier this year as Pakistan simultaneously embarked on a diplomatic effort to mediate between Iran and the United States.

items.title: Bodies of Nirmal Purja, 4 other climbers airlifted to Skardu after Broad Peak avalanche
items.description: Bodies of five more international climbers, including world-renowned British-Nepali Nirmal Purja, have been airlifted to Skardu after they were killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak, the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) said on Thursday. The avalanche struck on July 30, cutting off contact with the 10-member international expedition led by 43-year-old Purja on Broad Peak, one of the world’s highest mountains. His company confirmed there were no survivors . “Following one of the most technically demanding recovery operations on Broad Peak, the Alpine Club of Pakistan confirms that the bodies of Nirmal Purja, Wang Zhong, Nima Sherpa, Gyalu Sherpa, and Killi Pemba “Kilu” Sherpa have been transported to Skardu CMH Hospital by helicopter,” ACP said in its statement on Thursday. “Following necessary procedures and documentation, they will be transferred to Islamabad,” it said, adding that they have been prepared for repatriation to their respective home countries under special arrangements. ACP Secretary General Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that so far, seven bodies have been recovered and airlifted to Skardu. The search operation continues for the eighth day as Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi and American Sarah Mallory Geis remain missing. Shigri said remains believed to belong to Geis had been airlifted on Saturday along with bodies of two other climbers, but her body has still not been found. The body of Nawang Thindu Sherpa was spotted but could not be recovered due to its location in a high-altitude, avalanche-prone area, Naila Kiani of the ACP told Dawn . A Pakistan Army helicopter on Thursday brought the five bodies to Skardu, where they were received by ACP, Baltistan Commissioner Kamal Khan, army officers, civil administration officials, the tourism department, the district administration and local representatives. The participants paid tribute to the deceased climbers, acknowledged their contributions and expressed their condolences to the bereaved families. Later, all the bodies were transferred to the Combined Military Hospital (CMH) in Skardu, where the necessary legal formalities, documentation and identification procedures were completed, ACP said. The bodies were then placed in coffins, each draped with the national flag of the respective country before being accorded an official farewell with state honours. Officials said that the search and rescue operation was carried out under extremely challenging conditions. They praised the exceptional efforts of the local high-altitude porters, rescue personnel and mountaineers who took part in the operation, and also commended the rescue team’s professionalism and dedication. “Pakistan Army, local rescue teams and relevant agencies are participating in the search and rescue operation, and the search for the remaining missing mountaineers is continuing using all possible resources,” the ACP statement noted. The bodies of Purja, Wang, Nima Sherpa and Kili Pemba Sherpa had been recovered on Sunday and airlifted to the base camp on Wednesday. Previously, Gyalu Sherpa’s body had also been shifted to base camp. The five bodies could not be immediately moved from the base camp of Broad Peak as helicopter service was needed to airlift them, but bad weather had created difficulties in the transfer. The bodies of two other climbers, identified as Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy and Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung, had been recovered on Friday and their remains were later airlifted to Skardu.

items.title: La Centrafrique et le Cameroun apaisent les tensions après un incident à la frontière des deux pays
items.description: En Centrafrique, un nouvel incident ravive les tensions à la frontière avec le Cameroun. Samedi 1er août, deux gendarmes camerounais ont été interpellés dans le village de Gasol, à environ six kilomètres de la frontière, lors d’une opération que la partie centrafricaine qualifie d’illégale sur son territoire. Leur présence a été contestée par des habitants, avant l’intervention des Forces armées centrafricaines. Pour éviter une escalade, les autorités sécuritaires des deux pays ont rapidement engagé des discussions.

items.description: Le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, Dr Ibrahima Sy, a présidé, ce mercredi 5 août 2026, au Centre anti-poison sénégalais (CAP) de l’Hôpital de Fann, la cérémonie officielle de lancement des activités du laboratoire de toxicologie et de pharmacologie clinique. Réhabilité et doté d’équipements de dernière génération pour une enveloppe globale de 1,6 milliard de francs CFA, ce laboratoire permettra, selon une note de la tutelle publiée jeudi, d’améliorer le diagnostic des intoxications, de renforcer l’expertise médico-légale, la lutte contre le dopage, la recherche et la vigilance sanitaire. Il s’agit notamment d’un laboratoire mobile destiné à l’Agence sénégalaise de Réglementation pharmaceutique (ARP Sénégal) et d’un camion-atelier de maintenance biomédicale remis à la Direction des Équipements et de la Maintenance (MSHP). Ces investissements, réalisés avec l’appui de la Banque mondiale, contribuent, estime la tutelle, à la modernisation du système de santé et au renforcement de la sécurité sanitaire au Sénégal. M. items.title: As Iran war drags on, Americans are bracing for more chaos in Middle East, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.description: By Jason Lange and Simon Lewis WASHINGTON, Aug 6 (Reuters) - Five months into the U.S. war with Iran, Americans who expect the Middle East to slide toward chaos outnumber those who see the war bringing more stability by three to one, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. The six-day poll concluded on Monday, as Republican President Donald Trump again backed away from threatened "massive attacks" on Iran, underscoring uncertainty surrounding a conflict he initially predicted would bring a swift victory.
